Given the 3-week approach requires prolonged waiting, TEE-guided early cardioversion is preferred for a stable patient who wants cardioversion. Anticoagulation should continue for ≥4 weeks post-cardioversion regardless (cardioversion itself increases thrombus risk transiently).

**Q:** A 72-year-old man with permanent AF and EF 35% is on warfarin (INR 2.4) and digoxin. His ventricular rate is 105 bpm at rest and 145 with moderate exertion. Which rate-control regimen change is most appropriate?

A) Add diltiazem for better rate control
B) Increase digoxin dose
C) Switch warfarin to apixaban and add metoprolol
D) Add bisoprolol and target resting HR 60–80 bpm

**A:** D) Add bisoprolol and target resting HR 60–80 bpm

In AF with HFrEF, rate control targets are: resting HR < 80 bpm (lenient 80–110 is acceptable per RACE II trial). Beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol, carvedilol) are the preferred rate-control agents in HF — they also provide prognostic benefit. Non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) are CONTRAINDICATED in HFrEF (negative inotropy worsens failure). Digoxin has limited effect on exertional rate (does not work on AV node during sympathetic activation) and has a narrow therapeutic index. Switching to apixaban can be considered (superior to warfarin) but doesn't address rate control.

**Q:** A 65-year-old man has symptomatic persistent AF. He has been cardioverted twice. He is on flecainide for rhythm control. His echo shows mild LV hypertrophy (septal thickness 13mm) and EF 60%. An outpatient ECG shows PR 210ms, narrow QRS, no delta wave. His BP is 148/86. What is the BEST rhythm-control strategy at this point?

A) Continue flecainide — two cardioversions do not indicate drug failure
B) Switch to amiodarone for more effective rhythm control
C) Catheter ablation — superior to antiarrhythmic drugs for AF recurrence reduction
D) Switch to dofetilide — better evidence in structural heart disease

**A:** C) Catheter ablation — superior to antiarrhythmic drugs for AF recurrence reduction

Flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease (LV hypertrophy, reduced EF, CAD) — flecainide can provoke proarrhythmia (1C VT) in scarred/hypertrophied myocardium. This patient has LV hypertrophy + hypertension = structural disease. Amiodarone is the most effective antiarrhythmic but has significant long-term toxicity. Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation) has been shown in multiple RCTs (CABANA, CASTLE-AF, EAST-AFNET 4) to be superior to drug therapy for AF recurrence reduction, symptom improvement, and in HF patients, mortality. Given recurrent AF on flecainide, ablation is now the recommended next step.

**Q:** A 44-year-old woman with no structural heart disease has frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) at 28,000/24 hours on Holter. She is asymptomatic. Echo shows EF 50% (down from 62% two years ago). What is the most likely cause of her declining EF?

A) Coincidental viral myocarditis
B) Progression to arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy
C) PVC-induced cardiomyopathy
D) Hypertensive cardiomyopathy

**A:** C) PVC-induced cardiomyopathy

PVC-induced cardiomyopathy occurs when PVC burden exceeds 10,000–20,000/day (especially >15% of total beats) and is characterized by progressive LV systolic dysfunction. The dyssynchronous contraction pattern from frequent PVCs leads to maladaptive remodeling. This is a reversible cause of cardiomyopathy — catheter ablation of the PVC focus (often RVOT) results in EF recovery (reverse remodeling) in 80% of cases. This patient's 28,000 PVCs/day with declining EF is classic PVC-induced cardiomyopathy. Holter-confirmed PVC burden >15% with unexplained LV dysfunction should prompt ablation consideration.

**Q:** A 68-year-old man presents with sudden-onset palpitations and dyspnea. ECG shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 175 bpm. Vagal maneuvers do not terminate it. The Brugada criteria are applied and strongly suggest ventricular tachycardia. He is hemodynamically stable (BP 110/70). What is the most appropriate IMMEDIATE management?

A) Adenosine 6mg IV — may terminate if actually SVT with aberrancy
B) Synchronized DC cardioversion 200J
C) IV procainamide or IV amiodarone
D) IV verapamil — most effective for hemodynamically stable VT

**A:** C) IV procainamide or IV amiodarone

Stable wide-complex tachycardia that is likely VT: first-line pharmacological treatment is IV procainamide (superior efficacy with fewer side effects than lidocaine, CLASS I recommendation) or IV amiodarone. Verapamil is DANGEROUS in VT — it causes hemodynamic collapse if the rhythm is actually VT. Adenosine can be considered for SVT with aberrancy but is lower priority if VT is likely and can provoke VF. DC cardioversion is appropriate if the patient deteriorates hemodynamically. In stable WCT suspected VT: IV procainamide or amiodarone first-line; synchronized cardioversion if unstable or drug failure.

**Q:** A 25-year-old man has a syncopal episode during a football game. His ECG shows a QTc of 510ms. His father died suddenly at age 30. Gene panel shows a pathogenic variant in the KCNQ1 gene. What is the diagnosis and which triggers should specifically be avoided?

A) Long QT type 2 (LQT2) — avoid sudden auditory stimuli (alarm clocks, doorbells)
B) Long QT type 1 (LQT1) — avoid swimming and intense physical exercise
C) Long QT type 3 (LQT3) — arrhythmias occur at rest/sleep; restrict nocturnal activity
D) Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT) — avoid exercise and catecholamine surge

**A:** B) Long QT type 1 (LQT1) — avoid swimming and intense physical exercise

KCNQ1 mutations → LQT1. Trigger: exercise/swimming/emotional stress (adrenergic-mediated). The IKs channel (slow delayed rectifier K+ current encoded by KCNQ1) is most important during adrenergic stimulation — hence arrhythmias occur with exercise. LQT1 patients respond well to beta-blockers. LQT2 (KCNH2) — sudden auditory triggers. LQT3 (SCN5A) — arrhythmias at rest/sleep, bradycardia-dependent; mexiletine used. Swimming in cold water is particularly dangerous in LQT1 — vagal response + QTc prolongation. Beta-blockers are first-line therapy for LQT1.

**Q:** A 65-year-old woman with EF 38% and LBBB (QRS 165ms) undergoes CRT implantation. After the procedure, her 12-lead ECG shows a QRS of 145ms with a right bundle branch block pattern. Chest X-ray shows the LV lead in the anterolateral position. What does the RBBB pattern on ECG post-CRT suggest?

A) Successful LV pacing — RBBB pattern is expected when pacing from the LV
B) Lead dislodgement — the LV lead has migrated to the RV
C) Appropriate RV sensing with LV pacing only
D) Phrenic nerve stimulation — requires threshold reduction

**A:** A) Successful LV pacing — RBBB pattern is expected when pacing from the LV

When the LV is paced from a lateral or posterolateral vein (LV lateral wall), the electrical impulse travels from left to right — producing a RIGHT bundle branch block (RBBB) pattern on surface ECG, since the right ventricle is depolarized late. This is the expected appearance of successful LV pacing in CRT. If the lead were in the RV (dislodged), it would show a LEFT bundle branch block pattern. The narrowing of QRS from 165ms to 145ms and RBBB pattern confirm effective biventricular resynchronization.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man with structurally normal heart has atrial flutter with typical sawtooth flutter waves at 300 bpm. He is rate-controlled with a ventricular rate of 75. Which statement about typical atrial flutter is TRUE?

A) Typical flutter is a macro-re-entrant circuit through the crista terminalis in the left atrium
B) The CTI (cavotricuspid isthmus) is the critical slow zone; ablation of this achieves >95% cure rate
C) Anticoagulation is not required for flutter as thrombus formation is less common than in AF
D) Atrial flutter requires more aggressive rate control than AF due to risk of 1:1 conduction

**A:** B) The CTI (cavotricuspid isthmus) is the critical slow zone; ablation of this achieves >95% cure rate

Typical (isthmus-dependent) atrial flutter is a right atrial macro-re-entrant circuit rotating counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus. The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid valve — is the critical slow conduction zone. CTI ablation achieves >95% long-term cure rate and is the treatment of choice. Anticoagulation IS required for flutter — same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds as AF (thrombus can form in the LAA). Rate control is often more difficult in flutter — 2:1 conduction at 150 bpm is common; 1:1 conduction with AV conduction enhancers is dangerous.

**Q:** A 78-year-old woman has complete heart block (third-degree AV block) following inferior MI. Her escape rhythm is 42 bpm with a narrow QRS. Blood pressure is 88/60. She is symptomatic with presyncope. What is the most appropriate IMMEDIATE treatment?

A) Transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous pacing
B) Permanent pacemaker implantation within 24 hours
C) IV atropine 0.5mg — vagally-mediated AV block responds well
D) IV isoproterenol infusion to accelerate the escape rhythm

**A:** A) Transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous pacing

Complete AV block post-inferior MI is usually transient (RCA occlusion → ischemia of AV node) and may resolve within 1–2 weeks in up to 40% of cases. However, if hemodynamically unstable, TEMPORARY pacing is required immediately — transvenous temporary pacing is definitive, preceded by transcutaneous pacing as an immediate bridge. Atropine can accelerate AV nodal conduction in vagally-mediated (inferior MI) block — and is a reasonable initial pharmacological step, but with BP 88/60 and presyncope, the priority is transcutaneous pacing as the most reliable bridge. Permanent pacing can be reconsidered at 7–10 days if block does not resolve.

**Q:** A 70-year-old man with sick sinus syndrome has a dual-chamber pacemaker (DDD mode). His paced ECG shows a paced P wave followed by a native QRS. Over time, he develops RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy with EF falling from 60% to 38%. Which programming change or intervention is most appropriate?

A) Switch to VOO mode to avoid oversensing
B) Upgrade to CRT-P (biventricular pacemaker) if RV pacing >40%
C) Switch to AAI mode only — eliminate RV pacing entirely
D) No intervention — cardiomyopathy is not caused by RV pacing

**A:** B) Upgrade to CRT-P (biventricular pacemaker) if RV pacing >40%

RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy occurs when cumulative RV pacing burden >40% leads to dyssynchronous LV contraction (similar to LBBB physiology), causing progressive LV dysfunction. Management: (1) minimize RV pacing (program AV delay optimization or mode switch to AAI/AAIR in SSS with intact AV conduction); (2) if EF already reduced and RV pacing mandatory, upgrade to biventricular (CRT) pacing. The BLOCK-HF trial showed CRT superior to RV pacing in patients with AV block and mild-moderate LV dysfunction. With EF now 38%, CRT upgrade is strongly indicated.

**Q:** A 35-year-old woman has palpitations. A 14-day patch monitor shows frequent short bursts of narrow-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm that terminate abruptly with a P wave visible just after the QRS (RP interval < 70ms). What is the most likely mechanism?

A) Atrial tachycardia — focal automatic origin in right atrial appendage
B) AVNRT (typical slow-fast) — retrograde P wave near or within QRS
C) AVRT using accessory pathway — long RP tachycardia
D) Junctional ectopic tachycardia

**A:** B) AVNRT (typical slow-fast) — retrograde P wave near or within QRS

Typical AVNRT (slow-fast) is the most common cause of paroxysmal SVT in women. The circuit uses the slow pathway (antegrade) and fast pathway (retrograde). Retrograde atrial activation occurs nearly simultaneously with ventricular activation — hence the P wave is buried within or immediately after the QRS (RP interval < 70ms, often < 100ms). Short RP tachycardia differentials: AVNRT, AVRT with fast accessory pathway. Long RP tachycardia: atypical AVNRT, atrial tachycardia, PJRT. The pseudo-R' in V1 or pseudo-S in inferior leads is the buried retrograde P wave — pathognomonic of typical AVNRT.

**Q:** A 62-year-old man undergoes EP study for recurrent VT. Mapping reveals a scar in the inferior LV wall. During tachycardia, entrainment mapping from within the scar demonstrates a post-pacing interval (PPI) of 30ms above the tachycardia cycle length (TCL). What does this indicate and what ablation strategy should be used?

A) PPI = TCL + 30ms suggests this site is within the circuit; ablate here
B) PPI 30ms above TCL indicates this site is a bystander; ablate elsewhere
C) PPI < 20ms above TCL would be needed to indicate within the reentry circuit
D) PPI results are unreliable in scar-related VT — only activation mapping is valid

**A:** A) PPI = TCL + 30ms suggests this site is within the circuit; ablate here

During entrainment of a re-entrant VT: the post-pacing interval (PPI) reflects how far pacing is from the tachycardia circuit. PPI – TCL (the 'entrained interval') < 30ms indicates the pacing site is WITHIN or very close to the critical circuit isthmus — ablation here is likely effective. PPI – TCL of 30–50ms = within or near circuit. PPI – TCL > 50ms = bystander/remote site. The concealed entrainment concept (pacing at TCL without morphology change + PPI≈TCL) is the classic entrainment criterion for identifying the central isthmus. This site (PPI = TCL + 30ms) is within the circuit — ideal ablation target.

**Q:** A 48-year-old man with Brugada syndrome (Type 1 ECG pattern, spontaneous) has had one episode of syncope at rest. EP study is performed. Which finding during EP study would most support ICD implantation?

A) Inducible VF with a single premature extrastimulus
B) Inducible VF requiring triple extrastimuli — highly non-specific
C) Sinus node dysfunction on EP study
D) Prolonged HV interval > 100ms

**A:** D) Prolonged HV interval > 100ms

EP-guided ICD decision in Brugada is controversial. In the PRELUDE registry and consensus statements: (1) Inducibility of VF with 1–2 extrastimuli is more specific and relevant. (2) Triple extrastimuli induction is non-specific (high false positive). (3) An HV interval > 70ms (especially >100ms) indicates significant His-Purkinje disease and predicts worse prognosis with risk of AV block — supports ICD implantation. In a patient with spontaneous Type 1 Brugada + syncope (intermediate risk): EP study findings (particularly HV interval) and ICD are guided by risk stratification. Quinidine is an alternative to ICD in some patients.

**Q:** A 77-year-old man has symptomatic bradycardia from sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome) with no documented AV block. A permanent pacemaker is being considered. Which pacing mode is most appropriate to PREVENT pacemaker syndrome?

A) VVI — simple, appropriate for AF patients
B) VVIR — rate-responsive ventricular pacing
C) AAIR — rate-responsive atrial pacing only
D) DDDR — dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing with AV delay optimization

**A:** D) DDDR — dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing with AV delay optimization

Pacemaker syndrome (retrograde VA conduction → atrial contraction against closed AV valves → hypotension, cannon A waves, fatigue) occurs with VVI pacing due to AV dyssynchrony. DDDR (dual-chamber, dual-sense, dual-response, rate-responsive) maintains AV synchrony by sensing the atrium and pacing the ventricle after an appropriate AV delay — preventing retrograde VA conduction and pacemaker syndrome. In sick sinus syndrome without AV block, AAIR is physiologically ideal (preserves native AV conduction) but risks pacing failure if AV block develops. DDDR is the most comprehensive and guideline-preferred mode for SSS.

**Q:** A 60-year-old man on amiodarone for AF presents with exertional dyspnea over 3 months. PFTs show: TLC 68% predicted, DLCO 52% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.82. His chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities and peripheral consolidations. What is the most appropriate management?

A) Start high-dose prednisone — amiodarone pulmonary toxicity requires aggressive immunosuppression
B) Discontinue amiodarone and substitute with dofetilide
C) Discontinue amiodarone; add corticosteroids for severe cases; substitute with dronedarone if EF normal
D) Continue amiodarone at lower dose — the lung changes are likely non-specific

**A:** C) Discontinue amiodarone; add corticosteroids for severe cases; substitute with dronedarone if EF normal

Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity (APT) occurs in 2–7% of patients and is the most serious non-cardiac complication. Diagnosis: new pulmonary infiltrates + PFTs (restrictive pattern + reduced DLCO) + clinical context. Management: (1) Discontinue amiodarone — mandatory; (2) Corticosteroids for moderate-severe cases (prednisone 40–60 mg/day tapering over months — prevents fibrosis progression); (3) Alternative antiarrhythmic — dronedarone (if EF ≥ 35% and no decompensated HF), sotalol, or dofetilide. Dronedarone shares amiodarone structure but lacks iodine, reducing pulmonary/thyroid toxicity. Note: amiodarone has a 40–55 day half-life — effects persist weeks after stopping.

**Q:** What is the Vaughan-Williams classification of antiarrhythmic drugs?

**A:** Class I (Na channel): IA (procainamide), IB (lidocaine), IC (flecainide, propafenone). Class II: beta-blockers. Class III (K channel): amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide. Class IV: non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil)

Class IC: contraindicated in structural heart disease and post-MI (CAST trial: increased mortality). Class III: QT prolongation risk. Amiodarone: most effective but toxic (thyroid, pulmonary, hepatic, corneal, skin). Sotalol: class II+III, requires QT monitoring. Dronedarone: less toxic but less effective than amiodarone.

**Q:** How is atrial fibrillation rate vs rhythm control decided?

**A:** Rate control preferred for: asymptomatic/mildly symptomatic, elderly, persistent AF, significant comorbidities. Rhythm control preferred for: symptomatic despite rate control, young, paroxysmal, HFrEF (EAST-AFNET 4: early rhythm control may improve outcomes)

CCS AF guidelines. Rate control targets: <100 bpm resting (lenient) or <80 (strict - no difference per RACE II). Drugs: beta-blocker or diltiazem first-line. Digoxin adjunct only. Rhythm control: cardioversion, antiarrhythmics (flecainide for no structural HD, amiodarone/sotalol if structural), catheter ablation.

**Q:** How is the stroke risk assessed in AF and when is anticoagulation indicated?

**A:** CHA2DS2-VASc: CHF(1), HTN(1), Age>=75(2), DM(1), Stroke/TIA(2), Vascular disease(1), Age 65-74(1), Sex female(1). Score >=2 males or >=3 females: anticoagulate. Score 1 male: consider. 0: no anticoagulation

CCS recommends DOACs over warfarin (less ICH, no monitoring). Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edabigatran, edoxaban. LAA occlusion (Watchman) for patients who cannot tolerate long-term anticoagulation. HAS-BLED assesses bleeding risk but should NOT be used to withhold indicated anticoagulation.

**Q:** What is the approach to new-onset atrial fibrillation?

**A:** Assess hemodynamic stability. Unstable: cardioversion. Stable: rate control + anticoagulation assessment. Determine cause: thyroid, PE, sepsis, alcohol, post-surgical. Duration <48h: cardiovert or rate control. >48h or unknown: anticoagulate >=3wk before cardioversion or TEE-guided

CCS guidelines. New AF workup: ECG, TSH, CBC, lytes, echo (valvular disease, LA size, EF). Post-cardioversion: anticoagulate >=4wk regardless (atrial stunning). Long-term anticoagulation based on CHA2DS2-VASc. Lone AF in young: low stroke risk but still assess.

**Q:** What is Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and how is it managed?

**A:** ECG: short PR (<120ms), delta wave, wide QRS. Accessory pathway (bundle of Kent). Risk: rapid AF conducting via pathway causing VF. Treatment: catheter ablation (curative). Avoid AV nodal blockers (digoxin, CCB, adenosine) in pre-excited AF

WPW with AF: irregular wide-complex tachycardia. AV nodal blockers can paradoxically increase conduction via accessory pathway causing VF. Treat with procainamide or cardioversion. Asymptomatic WPW: risk stratification with EP study. High-risk features: short SPERRI (<250ms).

**Q:** What are the types and management of ventricular tachycardia?

**A:** Monomorphic VT: single QRS morphology, usually structural heart disease. Hemodynamically stable: IV amiodarone 150mg over 10min. Unstable: synchronized cardioversion. Pulseless VT: defibrillation. Polymorphic VT (Torsades): IV magnesium 2g, overdrive pacing

Post-MI VT: ICD indication. VT storm (>=3 episodes in 24h): amiodarone infusion + beta-blocker optimization + catheter ablation. Brugada syndrome: ICD for high-risk, avoid Na channel blockers/fever. Long QT: beta-blocker, avoid QT-prolonging drugs, ICD if high-risk.

**Q:** What are the indications for permanent pacemaker?

**A:** Symptomatic bradycardia (sinus node dysfunction with symptoms). Complete heart block or Mobitz II (even if asymptomatic). Symptomatic 2:1 block. Tachy-brady syndrome needing rate control drugs. Post-cardiac surgery with persistent block

Mobitz I (Wenckebach): usually benign, does NOT need pacemaker unless symptomatic. Pacemaker types: single chamber (VVI for AF + bradycardia), dual chamber (DDD for sinus node + AV node), CRT (for HF + LBBB). Complications: lead displacement, infection, pneumothorax, pacemaker syndrome.

**Q:** How is atrial flutter diagnosed and managed?

**A:** ECG: sawtooth flutter waves at ~300/min (best seen II, III, aVF, V1). Usually 2:1 block giving rate ~150. Unstable: cardioversion (lower energy than AF, 50-100J). Anticoagulation: same as AF based on CHA2DS2-VASc. Catheter ablation (CTI line) is curative

Atrial flutter has higher stroke risk than often appreciated - anticoagulate same as AF. Antiarrhythmics poorly effective. Catheter ablation of cavo-tricuspid isthmus is first-line for typical flutter (>95% success). Rate control more difficult than AF (often resistant to drugs).

**Q:** What is the approach to syncope evaluation?

**A:** History most important: prodrome, triggers, position, witnesses. Cardiac syncope (high-risk): exertional, supine, palpitations, FHx sudden death, structural HD, abnormal ECG. Vasovagal: standing/pain trigger, prodrome, young. Workup: ECG (all), echo if structural suspected, Holter/loop if arrhythmic

Canadian Cardiovascular Society syncope guidelines. Admit if: suspected cardiac cause, significant injury, high-risk features. Tilt table test for recurrent suspected vasovagal. Implantable loop recorder for recurrent unexplained. Driving restrictions: CCS guidelines vary by cause (cardiac syncope: typically 3-12mo restriction).

**Q:** What is catheter ablation and for which arrhythmias is it indicated?

**A:** AF: PVI (pulmonary vein isolation) for symptomatic paroxysmal AF, increasingly first-line for persistent and HF. Atrial flutter: CTI ablation (curative >95%). SVT (AVNRT/AVRT): curative >95%. WPW: pathway ablation. VT: for recurrent VT/VT storm

CCS recommends ablation as first-line or early therapy for many supraventricular arrhythmias. AF ablation: PVI using radiofrequency or cryoballoon. Success: ~70-80% for paroxysmal AF. Complications: stroke, tamponade, PV stenosis, esophageal injury (rare). CASTLE-AF: ablation improves mortality in HFrEF+AF.

**Q:** What is the systematic approach to ECG interpretation?

**A:** Rate, rhythm, axis, intervals (PR, QRS, QT), P waves, ST/T changes, Q waves. Normal: rate 60-100, regular, axis -30 to +90, PR 120-200ms, QRS <120ms, QTc <440ms(M)/<460ms(F)

Critical findings to identify immediately: STEMI (ST elevation in contiguous leads), complete heart block, wide complex tachycardia, hyperkalemia (peaked T), PE (S1Q3T3, right heart strain).

**Q:** A 70-year-old male with a history of aortic stenosis experiences sudden loss of consciousness while climbing stairs. He regained consciousness within 30 seconds. What type of syncope is this, and why is it high-risk?

**A:** Cardiac syncope (exertional syncope due to fixed obstruction from aortic stenosis). This is high-risk because it indicates the cardiac output cannot meet demand, and it is associated with sudden cardiac death. Urgent echocardiography and cardiology consultation are required.

Syncope during exertion is cardiac until proven otherwise and should never be attributed to vasovagal. Other high-risk features include syncope while supine, preceding palpitations, family history of sudden death, and abnormal ECG. The Canadian Syncope Risk Score helps stratify patients in the ED.

**Q:** How do you differentiate cardiac syncope from vasovagal syncope from orthostatic hypotension based on history?

**A:** Vasovagal: prodrome (lightheadedness, warmth, nausea, diaphoresis), triggered by prolonged standing/emotional stress/pain, gradual onset, rapid full recovery. Cardiac: sudden onset without prodrome, exertional, preceding palpitations, family history of sudden death. Orthostatic: occurs on standing, associated with volume depletion, medications (antihypertensives), or autonomic dysfunction.

Orthostatic hypotension is confirmed by a drop of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. Vasovagal is the most common cause of syncope overall, but cardiac causes carry the highest mortality risk and must always be excluded first.

**Q:** What investigations should be ordered for a patient presenting with syncope of unclear etiology?

**A:** Initial workup: 12-lead ECG (all patients), orthostatic vitals, CBC, glucose, electrolytes, troponin (if cardiac suspected). Extended: echocardiography (structural heart disease), Holter monitor (24-48h) or event recorder (paroxysmal arrhythmia), tilt-table test (recurrent vasovagal suspected), implantable loop recorder (recurrent unexplained syncope).

ECG is the single most important initial test and can reveal arrhythmias, long QT, Brugada pattern, WPW, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Holter monitors capture 24-48 hours continuously but miss infrequent events. Implantable loop recorders can monitor for up to 3 years for rare but recurrent episodes.

**Q:** A 25-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of syncope in crowded, warm environments preceded by nausea and tunnel vision. Each episode lasts <1 minute with full recovery. Cardiac workup is normal. What is the diagnosis and management?

**A:** Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) syncope. Management: patient education, recognition and avoidance of triggers, counter-pressure maneuvers (leg crossing, hand gripping), adequate hydration and salt intake. Tilt-table testing can confirm the diagnosis. Midodrine may be considered for refractory cases.

Vasovagal syncope results from a paradoxical reflex causing bradycardia and vasodilation. It is benign but can significantly impact quality of life. Physical counter-pressure maneuvers have the strongest evidence for prevention and can abort an impending episode if performed during the prodrome.

**Q:** How do you identify RBBB vs LBBB on ECG?

**A:** RBBB: rsR' in V1-V2 (M-shaped), wide S in I/V6. LBBB: broad notched R in I/V5-V6, QS or rS in V1. Both: QRS >120ms

New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI (Sgarbossa criteria if STEMI suspected in LBBB). RBBB: often benign but can indicate RV strain (PE). LBBB: usually pathological (HTN, cardiomyopathy).

**Q:** What ECG leads correspond to which coronary territories?

**A:** Anterior (V1-V4): LAD. Inferior (II,III,aVF): RCA. Lateral (I,aVL,V5-V6): LCx. Posterior: tall R in V1-V2 (mirror image). RV: ST elevation V4R

Reciprocal changes increase specificity for STEMI. Inferior STEMI: always get right-sided leads (V4R) to check for RV involvement — avoid nitrates and volume depletion if RV infarct.

**Q:** What is the WPW pattern on ECG and why is it dangerous?

**A:** Short PR (<120ms), delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), wide QRS. Danger: AF with rapid conduction down accessory pathway can cause VF. AVOID AV nodal blockers (adenosine, CCB, digoxin, beta-blockers)

WPW + AF: treat with procainamide or electrical cardioversion. AV nodal blockers enhance accessory pathway conduction. Definitive treatment: catheter ablation of accessory pathway.

**Q:** What are the causes of left axis deviation (LAD) and right axis deviation (RAD) on ECG?

**A:** LAD (axis < -30°): left anterior fascicular block, inferior MI, LVH, WPW (posterior pathway). RAD (axis > +90°): right ventricular hypertrophy, left posterior fascicular block, PE, lateral MI, COPD, pediatric normal variant.

LAD is most commonly caused by left anterior fascicular block, which shifts the axis leftward because the remaining left posterior fascicle depolarizes the ventricle from inferior to superior. RAD is less common and left posterior fascicular block is a diagnosis of exclusion, as it requires ruling out RVH and other causes.

**Q:** What are the ECG criteria for right bundle branch block (RBBB) versus left bundle branch block (LBBB)?

**A:** RBBB: QRS ≥120 ms, rsR' pattern in V1-V2 (M-shaped), wide slurred S in I and V6. LBBB: QRS ≥120 ms, broad notched R in I, aVL, V5-V6, absent Q in I and V6, rS or QS in V1.

RBBB can be a normal finding or indicate right heart strain (PE, RVH). New LBBB is always pathological and may indicate acute MI (per Sgarbossa criteria), cardiomyopathy, or conduction disease. LBBB makes standard ST-segment interpretation unreliable for MI diagnosis.

**Q:** Which ECG leads correspond to which coronary artery territories: anterior, inferior, and lateral MI?

**A:** Anterior (V1-V4): LAD. Inferior (II, III, aVF): RCA (85%) or LCx (15%). Lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6): LCx. Posterior: reciprocal ST depression in V1-V3, tall R waves in V1.

Anterior STEMI from proximal LAD occlusion carries the highest mortality due to large area of myocardium at risk. Inferior MI should prompt a right-sided ECG (V4R) to assess for RV involvement, which changes fluid management. Posterior MI is easily missed without posterior leads (V7-V9).

**Q:** How do you differentiate pericarditis from STEMI on ECG?

**A:** Pericarditis: diffuse concave-up ST elevation, PR depression (especially in II), ST elevation in lead II > III, no reciprocal changes, Spodick sign (downsloping TP segment). STEMI: convex or straight ST elevation in a coronary territory, reciprocal ST depression, pathological Q waves.

The ratio of ST elevation to T-wave amplitude in V6 >0.25 favors pericarditis over early repolarization. PR depression is the most specific ECG finding for pericarditis. STEMI has reciprocal changes (e.g., inferior ST elevation with lateral ST depression), which pericarditis lacks.

**Q:** What is Wellens syndrome, and why is it a critical ECG diagnosis?

**A:** Wellens syndrome shows biphasic T waves (Type A) or deep symmetric T-wave inversions (Type B) in V2-V3 during pain-free intervals, indicating critical proximal LAD stenosis. Stress testing is contraindicated.

Wellens pattern represents a pre-infarction state with >90% proximal LAD stenosis. These patients are at high risk for extensive anterior MI without intervention. Troponin may be normal or minimally elevated. The pattern appears when the patient is pain-free, not during active ischemia.

**Q:** What is the de Winter ECG pattern, and what does it signify?

**A:** De Winter pattern shows upsloping ST depression at the J-point with tall, symmetric T waves in precordial leads (V1-V6), often with subtle ST elevation in aVR. It represents acute LAD occlusion and is a STEMI equivalent.

De Winter pattern is present in ~2% of acute LAD occlusions and does not evolve into classic ST elevation. It should be treated with emergent PCI despite not meeting traditional STEMI criteria. It is important to recognize because these patients may be triaged incorrectly as NSTEMI.

**Q:** What are the common causes of prolonged QTc, and how is torsades de pointes managed?

**A:** Causes: drugs (antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, congenital long QT. Torsades management: IV magnesium 2g, overdrive pacing, isoproterenol; avoid further QT-prolonging drugs.

QTc >500 ms significantly increases torsades risk. Magnesium is effective even with normal serum levels. Overdrive pacing at 90-110 bpm shortens the QT interval and suppresses the pause-dependent triggered activity. Standard antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, procainamide) are contraindicated as they prolong QT further.

**Q:** What are the ECG findings in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, and what is the dangerous arrhythmia to watch for?

**A:** WPW: short PR interval (<120 ms), delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), widened QRS. The dangerous arrhythmia is pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation.

In WPW, an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node, allowing rapid conduction. AV nodal blockers (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, adenosine) are contraindicated in pre-excited AF as they may enhance accessory pathway conduction. Procainamide or electrical cardioversion are appropriate treatments.

**Q:** How do you distinguish digoxin effect from digoxin toxicity on ECG?

**A:** Digoxin effect (therapeutic): ST scooping ('Salvador Dali mustache'), shortened QTc, flattened/inverted T waves. Digoxin toxicity: any arrhythmia, classically bidirectional VT, accelerated junctional rhythm, atrial tachycardia with block, frequent PVCs.

Digoxin effect on ECG does not indicate toxicity. Digoxin toxicity is diagnosed clinically (nausea, visual changes, arrhythmias) and by elevated levels (>2.0 ng/mL). Hypokalemia predisposes to toxicity despite normal drug levels. Treatment of severe toxicity is digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind/DigiFab).

**Q:** What are the ECG findings in Brugada syndrome, and what are the two types of Brugada patterns?

**A:** Type 1 (diagnostic): coved ST elevation ≥2 mm in V1-V3 with negative T wave. Type 2 (suggestive): saddleback ST elevation in V1-V3 with positive/biphasic T wave. Type 1 is required for diagnosis.

Brugada syndrome is a sodium channelopathy causing sudden cardiac death from polymorphic VT/VF, typically in young males during sleep or fever. Type 2 pattern requires provocation with ajmaline or procainamide to convert to Type 1 for diagnosis. An ICD is the only proven treatment to prevent sudden death.

**Q:** What are the Sgarbossa criteria for diagnosing acute MI in the setting of LBBB?

**A:** Original Sgarbossa: (1) concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm (5 points), (2) concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1-V3 (3 points), (3) discordant ST elevation ≥5 mm (2 points). Score ≥3 is specific for MI. Modified Sgarbossa replaces criterion 3 with ST/S ratio ≥0.25.

LBBB makes standard ST-segment analysis unreliable because baseline repolarization is altered. Concordant ST changes (same direction as QRS) are highly specific for acute MI. The modified Smith-Sgarbossa criteria using the ST/S ratio improve sensitivity without sacrificing specificity.

**Q:** What ECG findings suggest hyperkalemia, and at what potassium levels do they typically appear?

**A:** K+ 5.5-6.5: peaked T waves. K+ 6.5-7.5: prolonged PR, flattened P waves, QRS widening. K+ 7.5-8.0: sine wave pattern. K+ >8.0: VF/asystole.

The progression is predictable but individual variation exists; some patients develop lethal arrhythmias at lower levels. IV calcium gluconate stabilizes the myocardial membrane within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin/dextrose, bicarbonate, and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly, while kayexalate and dialysis remove it.

**Q:** A patient presents with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm. What diagnosis should you consider, and what is the initial management?

**A:** A rate of exactly 150 bpm should raise suspicion for atrial flutter with 2:1 block. Initial management: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push to unmask flutter waves if diagnosis uncertain. If flutter confirmed, rate control or cardioversion.

Atrial flutter has an atrial rate of ~300 bpm, so 2:1 block produces a ventricular rate of ~150 bpm. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction, revealing sawtooth flutter waves in II, III, aVF. Unlike SVT, adenosine will not terminate flutter but helps with diagnosis.

**Q:** What are the ECG findings of right ventricular MI, and how does it change management of an inferior STEMI?

**A:** ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R (right-sided ECG) with inferior ST elevation. Management: avoid nitrates and diuretics (preload-dependent), give IV fluids for hypotension, and pursue emergent PCI.

The RV is preload-dependent, so nitrates and diuretics can cause catastrophic hypotension by reducing venous return. RV infarction complicates ~30-50% of inferior MIs and is associated with higher mortality. Hypotension in inferior MI should prompt immediate right-sided ECG.

**Q:** What is the approach to differentiating wide-complex tachycardia as VT versus SVT with aberrancy?

**A:** Favor VT: AV dissociation, fusion/capture beats, concordance in precordial leads, northwest axis, Brugada criteria positive, history of structural heart disease. If uncertain, treat as VT (safer assumption).

VT accounts for ~80% of wide-complex tachycardias, especially in patients with prior MI or cardiomyopathy. The Brugada algorithm (not syndrome) uses a stepwise approach: RS absence in all precordial leads, RS interval >100 ms, AV dissociation, and morphology criteria. Adenosine should be avoided if VT is suspected.

**Q:** What are the ECG hallmarks of atrial fibrillation (AFib)?

**A:** Absent P waves, may have fibrillatory waves, irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm

AFib results from chaotic atrial electrical activity, causing an irregularly irregular heartbeat.

**Q:** What defines first-degree AV block on ECG?

**A:** Fixed, prolonged P-R interval (>200 msec), but every P wave has a QRS following it

First-degree block indicates slowed AV conduction but no dropped beats.

**Q:** What characterizes second-degree Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) AV block?

**A:** Gradual prolongation of the P-R interval precedes a dropped QRS complex (non-conducted P wave)

Wenckebach blocks typically occur at the AV node level and are often benign and reversible.

**Q:** What characterizes second-degree Mobitz Type II (Hay) AV block?

**A:** Fixed P-R interval with a consistent ratio of atrial to dropped ventricular beats (e.g., 3:1 = 3 atrial beats for every 1 ventricular beat)

Mobitz II blocks occur distal to the AV node and are more dangerous than Mobitz I, often requiring pacing.

**Q:** What ECG findings indicate third-degree (complete) AV block?

**A:** Constant P-P and R-R intervals but variable P-R intervals; P waves and QRS complexes are independent

Complete heart block results from complete interruption of conduction between atria and ventricles.

**Q:** What ECG findings characterize trifascicular block?

**A:** Long PR segment (first-degree AV block) combined with bifascicular block (typically RBBB + left anterior or posterior fascicular block)

Trifascicular block indicates disease in all three fascicles and carries risk of progression to complete heart block.

**Q:** What are the ECG findings characteristic of third-degree (complete) AV block?

**A:** Wide or narrow QRS, constant P-P and R-R intervals with variable PR intervals, and no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes ('P waves marching through'), with more P waves than QRS complexes

In complete heart block, the atria and ventricles beat independently because no impulses conduct through the AV node. An escape pacemaker distal to the block initiates ventricular depolarization.

**Q:** What ECG findings differentiate atrial flutter from atrial fibrillation?

**A:** Atrial flutter shows 'sawtooth' flutter waves (250-350 bpm, usually 300 bpm) with regular or regularly irregular ventricular response, while AFib shows absent P waves with fibrillatory baseline and irregularly irregular ventricular response

The 'sawtooth' pattern of atrial flutter is due to macro-reentry circuit in the right atrium, typically involving the isthmus between the tricuspid annulus and IVC.

**Q:** What is the most common sustained arrhythmia?

**A:** Atrial fibrillation (AFib)

AFib is the most prevalent sustained cardiac arrhythmia worldwide, with increasing prevalence with age and associated cardiovascular conditions.

**Q:** How does 'lone' AFib differ from other types?

**A:** 'Lone' AFib occurs in persons under 65 years with no clinical or echocardiographic causes identified

Patients with lone AFib have better prognosis as they lack structural heart disease or other identifiable triggers that promote arrhythmia recurrence.

**Q:** What are the ECG findings in atrial fibrillation?

**A:** No organized P waves (chaotic fibrillatory baseline from rapid atrial activity at 350-600 bpm) and irregularly irregular ventricular response

The AV node irregularly filters incoming atrial impulses, producing the characteristic irregularly irregular rhythm without discernible atrial activity.

**Q:** What is the typical atrial rate in atrial flutter and why does it cause variable AV block?

**A:** Atrial rate is 250-350 bpm (usually 300 bpm); AV block usually occurs because the AV node cannot conduct all atrial impulses, resulting in 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 block

The AV node's refractory period protects the ventricles from excessively rapid rates. Fixed or variable block ratios determine ventricular rate.

**Q:** What is the concern with combining non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem) with beta-blockers?

**A:** Risk of symptomatic sinus bradycardia or AV block due to combined negative chronotropic effects

Both drug classes suppress cardiac conduction, and the combination can cause dangerous bradyarrhythmias requiring pacemaker placement.

**Q:** What is the hallmark ECG finding in third-degree (complete) AV block?

**A:** P waves and QRS complexes are completely dissociated with no relationship between them (P waves 'march through' the QRS complexes). There are more P waves than QRS complexes, and PR intervals vary randomly.

Third-degree AV block represents complete failure of conduction from atria to ventricles. The ventricles are driven by an escape pacemaker distal to the block, which may be narrow or wide depending on its location.

**Q:** What is the management approach for third-degree AV block?

**A:** Permanent electrical pacing (pacemaker) is the definitive treatment for symptomatic third-degree AV block.

Patients with third-degree AV block are at high risk for syncope and sudden cardiac death due to unreliable ventricular conduction. A pacemaker ensures reliable heart rate.

**Q:** What are the characteristic ECG findings of atrial flutter?

**A:** 'Sawtooth' flutter waves (best seen in inferior leads II, III, aVF), narrow QRS complexes (unless aberrancy exists), and atrial rate of 250-350 bpm (usually 300 bpm). AV block is usually present (commonly 2:1, giving a ventricular rate of ~150 bpm).

Atrial flutter results from a macro re-entry circuit in the right atrium, typically involving the isthmus between the tricuspid annulus and IVC. Carotid massage or adenosine can slow AV conduction to better visualize the flutter waves.

**Q:** What is 'lone' atrial fibrillation?

**A:** AF occurring in persons under 65 years of age with no clinical or echocardiographic evidence of underlying heart disease.

Lone AF carries a lower thromboembolic risk than AF with structural heart disease, though anticoagulation decisions still require individual risk assessment.

**Q:** What is the mechanism of atrial fibrillation maintenance?

**A:** Tachycardia causes atrial structural and electrophysiological remodeling. The longer a patient remains in AF, the more the atria remodel, creating more substrate for AF maintenance - making it progressively harder to restore normal sinus rhythm.

This concept of 'AF begets AF' explains why early intervention (rhythm control) may be beneficial and why anticoagulation becomes increasingly important with longer AF duration.

**Q:** What caution is needed when combining verapamil/diltiazem with beta-blockers?

**A:** May cause symptomatic sinus bradycardia or AV block

Both drug classes suppress cardiac conduction, and their combination can cause dangerous bradyarrhythmias.

**Q:** What are the advantages of TAVR over SAVR in intermediate-risk patients with aortic stenosis?

**A:** TAVR resulted in larger aortic valve areas, lower rates of AKI, less severe bleeding, and less new-onset atrial fibrillation

The transcatheter approach demonstrated benefits in renal protection and bleeding complications, though surgical replacement showed advantages in vascular complications and paravalvular regurgitation.

**Q:** What are the key side effects of digoxin?

**A:** Bidirectional VT, bradyarrhythmias, AV block, blurred or yellow vision (van Gogh syndrome), anorexia, nausea/vomiting

Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index. Visual changes and arrhythmias are particularly concerning signs of toxicity.

**Q:** What are the side effects of beta-blockers used as antiarrhythmics?

**A:** Bronchospasm, negative inotropy, bradycardia, AV block, impotence, fatigue

Beta-blockers are contraindicated in severe bradycardia, AV block, decompensated heart failure, and severe asthma.

**Q:** What serious arrhythmia can Class III antiarrhythmics cause?

**A:** Torsades de Pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT prolongation)

The QT-prolonging effect of Class III drugs predisposes to Torsades de Pointes, particularly in patients with hypokalemia or congenital long QT.

**Q:** What are the side effects of verapamil and diltiazem?

**A:** Bradycardia, AV block, and hypotension

Class IV antiarrhythmics should be avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to their negative inotropic effects.

**Q:** In which clinical scenarios would you use dabigatran versus warfarin?

**A:** Dabigatran is used for AFib and venous thrombosis/PE in patients without severe renal impairment or recent surgery. Warfarin is preferred for patients with mechanical heart valves and those requiring frequent INR monitoring.

DOACs (including dabigatran) are generally preferred for non-valvular AFib due to lower bleeding risk and no monitoring requirement, but warfarin remains standard for mechanical valves.

**Q:** What are the contraindications for digoxin?

**A:** 2nd or 3rd degree AV block, AV junctional tachycardia, bidirectional VT, bradyarrhythmias, hypokalemia, blurred or yellow vision (van Gogh syndrome)

Digoxin's vagotonic effects on the AV node make it dangerous in conditions with pre-existing conduction abnormalities.

**Q:** What are the beta-blocker antiarrhythmics (Class II) and their side effects?

**A:** Propranolol, metoprolol, and others. Side effects: bronchospasm, negative inotropy, bradycardia, AV block, impotence, fatigue

Class II antiarrhythmics decrease phase 4 spontaneous depolarization. Used for SVT and AFib rate control.

**Q:** What are the Class IV antiarrhythmic drugs (calcium channel blockers)?

**A:** Verapamil SR and diltiazem. Side effects: bradycardia, AV block, hypotension

Class IV drugs slow phase 4 spontaneous depolarization and slow AV node conduction. Used for AFib rate control.

**Q:** What does the 2020 Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society guideline cover?

**A:** Comprehensive Guidelines for the Management of Atrial Fibrillation

**Q:** What are the contraindications to digoxin?

**A:** 2nd or 3rd degree AV block, AV block with junctional tachycardia, bidirectional VT, bradyarrhythmias, hypokalemia, blurred or yellow vision (van Gogh syndrome)

Digoxin can worsen AV block and is contraindicated in conduction abnormalities. Visual changes and hypokalemia increase toxicity risk.

**Q:** What are the side effects of beta-blockers as antiarrhythmics?

**A:** Bronchospasm, negative inotropy, bradycardia, AV block, impotence, fatigue

Non-selective beta-blockade affects both cardiac (beta-1) and pulmonary (beta-2) receptors, causing these well-known adverse effects.

**Q:** What are the side effects of Class IV antiarrhythmics?

**A:** Bradycardia, AV block, hypotension

Verapamil and diltiazem can cause significant bradycardia and conduction abnormalities. Verapamil has more negative inotropic effects than diltiazem.

**Q:** What is the Canadian approach to managing atrial fibrillation according to the 2020 CCS/CHRS guidelines?

**A:** Comprehensive guidelines covering anticoagulation, rhythm control, rate control, and catheter ablation

The 2020 Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations for AF management.

**Q:** Which organization publishes the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) Guidelines for atrial fibrillation management?

**A:** Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) in partnership with Canadian Heart Rhythm Society (CHRS)

The 2020 CCS/CHRS comprehensive guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for atrial fibrillation management tailored to Canadian clinical practice, including anticoagulation, rate/rhythm control, and catheter ablation strategies.

**Q:** What are the ECG findings in hyperkalemia?

**A:** Peaked narrow T waves, decreased P wave, prolonged PR interval, widening QRS, sine wave pattern, AV block, ventricular fibrillation, bradycardia

Progressive ECG changes reflect potassium's effects on cardiac conduction, from early peaked T waves to fatal dysrhythmias.

**Q:** What are the complications of hypothermia?

**A:** Coagulopathy, acidosis, dysrhythmias (AFib, VFib, profound bradycardia, asystole), and volume/electrolyte depletion

Cold diuresis causes volume depletion; cardiac irritability increases with decreasing temperature

**Q:** What ECG findings are characteristic of hyperkalemia?

**A:** Peaked/narrow T wave, decreased P wave, prolonged PR interval, widening of QRS, sine wave, AV block, VFib, bradycardia.

Hyperkalemia causes life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias. Peaked T waves are the earliest sign.

**Q:** What are complications of hypothermia?

**A:** Coagulopathy, acidosis, dysrhythmias (AFib, VFib, profound bradycardia, asystole), volume/electrolyte depletion

Cold diuresis leads to volume depletion; core temperature affects all organ systems.

**Q:** What are the serious adverse events that were significantly increased in the intensive BP arm of the ACCORD trial?

**A:** Bradycardia or arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, p=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, p=0.01)

Intensive BP control to <120 mmHg was associated with significantly more adverse events including bradycardia/arrhythmia and hyperkalemia compared to standard therapy.

**Q:** What serious adverse events were significantly increased with intensive BP control in ACCORD?

**A:** All serious adverse events (3.3% vs 1.27%, P<0.001), particularly bradycardia/arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, P=0.01)

Intensive BP control in T2DM required more medications (3.4 vs 2.1 at 1 year) and caused significantly more adverse events.

**Q:** What serious adverse events were increased with intensive BP control in ACCORD?

**A:** Bradycardia/arrhythmia and hyperkalemia

Serious adverse events: bradycardia/arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, P=0.01).

**Q:** What were the side effects of intensive BP control in the ACCORD trial?

**A:** Increased serious adverse events (3.3% vs. 1.27%, P<0.001), specifically bradycardia/arrhythmia (0.5% vs. 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs. 0.04%, P=0.01)

The intensive BP arm required more medications (mean 3.4 vs. 2.1 at 1 year) and had significantly more adverse events, though these were not the primary outcome.

**Q:** What serious adverse events were more common with intensive BP control in ACCORD?

**A:** Bradycardia or arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, P=0.01) were significantly more common with intensive BP therapy.

The ACCORD BP trial showed intensive treatment increased all serious adverse events (3.3% vs 1.27%, P<0.001), highlighting the risks of aggressive BP lowering in T2DM with CV risk factors.

**Q:** What serious adverse events were more common with intensive blood pressure therapy in the ACCORD BP Trial?

**A:** Bradycardia/arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, P=0.01)

Intensive BP therapy (sBP <120 mmHg) required more medications (3.4 vs 2.1 at 1 year) and had higher rates of serious adverse events overall (3.3% vs 1.27%, P<0.001)

**Q:** In the ACCORD BP trial, what serious adverse events were significantly more common with intensive BP control?

**A:** Intensive BP control (<120 mmHg) was associated with significantly more bradycardia or arrhythmia (0.5% vs 0.13%, P=0.02) and hyperkalemia (0.4% vs 0.04%, P=0.01).

The intensive arm used a mean of 3.4 medications at 1 year vs 2.1 in the standard arm, leading to more serious adverse events overall (3.3% vs 1.27%, P<0.001).

**Q:** According to the Vaughan-Williams classification, which class of antiarrhythmic drug prolongs phase 3 repolarization by blocking K+ channels, and what is a major adverse effect?

**A:** Class III (e.g., amiodarone, sotalol); major adverse effect is Torsades de Pointes (and for amiodarone: pulmonary toxicity, thyroid disease, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity)

Class III agents block K+ channels, prolonging the action potential and refractory period. Amiodarone also has class I, II, and IV properties. The prolonged QT interval predisposes to Torsades de Pointes, particularly with sotalol.

**Q:** A patient on procainamide (Class Ia antiarrhythmic) develops arthralgia, rash, and positive ANA. What is the likely adverse effect?

**A:** Drug-induced lupus (lupus-like syndrome)

Procainamide is classically associated with drug-induced lupus, which occurs in up to 30% of patients on long-term therapy. The syndrome resolves upon discontinuation. Class Ia agents also risk Torsades de Pointes.

**Q:** Which antiarrhythmic class includes lidocaine, and in what clinical scenario is IV lidocaine used?

**A:** Class Ib; IV lidocaine is used for ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., VT) in the acute setting

Class Ib agents mildly block Na+ channels and shorten phase 3 repolarization. Lidocaine is primarily used for acute ventricular arrhythmias. CNS toxicity (confusion, stupor, seizures) can occur with high doses.

**Q:** What is the mechanism of Class IV antiarrhythmics (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) and what are their main indications?

**A:** Calcium channel blockers; slow phase 4 spontaneous depolarization and AV node conduction. Used for SVT and rate control in AFib

Class IV agents block Ca2+ channels in the AV node, slowing conduction and ventricular rate. They are negative inotropes and chronotropes; major adverse effects include bradycardia, AV block, and hypotension. They are contraindicated in decompensated HF.

**Q:** AFFIRM trial compared rate control vs. rhythm control for AFib. What was the key conclusion?

**A:** No significant difference in mortality between rate control and rhythm control strategies for AFib

AFFIRM (NEJM 2002) demonstrated that rhythm control with antiarrhythmics was not superior to rate control in terms of mortality, and was associated with more hospitalizations and adverse drug events. Rate control is generally preferred as initial strategy for most AFib patients.

**Q:** ARISTOTLE trial compared apixaban vs. warfarin in AFib with additional stroke risk factors. What were the key findings?

**A:** Apixaban reduced stroke/systemic embolism, major bleeding, and mortality compared to warfarin in AFib

ARISTOTLE (NEJM 2011) demonstrated apixaban 5mg BID reduced stroke (1.27% vs. 1.60%/yr), major bleeding (2.13% vs. 3.09%/yr), and hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin. Canadian guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin for non-valvular AFib stroke prevention.

**Q:** RE-LY trial compared two doses of dabigatran (110 mg vs. 150 mg BID) against warfarin for stroke prevention in AFib. What was the conclusion?

**A:** Dabigatran 150 mg BID was superior to warfarin for stroke reduction; 110 mg was non-inferior with less major bleeding than warfarin

RE-LY (NEJM 2009) showed 150 mg dabigatran reduced stroke to 1.17%/yr vs. 1.69%/yr with warfarin, while 110 mg had lower major bleeding (2.71% vs. 3.36%/yr). In Canada, 150 mg is standard; 110 mg is used in elderly or high-bleeding-risk patients.

**Q:** ROCKET-AF compared rivaroxaban to warfarin in nonvalvular AFib. What was concluded about rivaroxaban's efficacy and bleeding profile?

**A:** Rivaroxaban was non-inferior to warfarin for stroke/systemic embolism prevention, with similar major bleeding rates

ROCKET-AF (NEJM 2011) demonstrated rivaroxaban 20 mg daily was non-inferior to warfarin for stroke prevention in nonvalvular AFib, with a trend toward reduction in hemorrhagic stroke. Unlike apixaban (ARISTOTLE), major bleeding was similar between groups.

**Q:** The ETOH-AFib trial studied alcohol abstinence in AFib patients who drink >10 standard drinks/week. What was demonstrated?

**A:** Alcohol abstinence significantly reduced AFib recurrence rates (53% vs. 73%) and AFib burden over 6 months

ETOH-AFib (NEJM 2020) provided evidence that alcohol cessation is a modifiable risk factor for AFib secondary prevention, reducing recurrence by nearly half. This supports lifestyle modification counseling as part of AFib management in Canadian clinical practice.

**Q:** A Class Ic antiarrhythmic drug (e.g., flecainide, propafenone) is being considered. What is the major adverse effect that limits their use in structural heart disease?

**A:** Proarrhythmic effect — Exacerbation of ventricular tachycardia (VT); all Class Ic agents also cause negative inotropy and bradycardia/heart block

The CAST trial demonstrated that flecainide and encainide increased mortality in post-MI patients with asymptomatic ventricular arrhythmias, establishing that Class Ic agents are contraindicated in structural heart disease. They are reserved for patients with structurally normal hearts (e.g., lone AFib).

**Q:** What is the clinical significance of amiodarone's multi-class antiarrhythmic properties?

**A:** Amiodarone has Class I, II, III, and IV properties — making it broadly effective but also increasing its adverse effect profile (pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, Torsades de Pointes)

As a Class III agent, amiodarone blocks K+ channels and prolongs repolarization; it also blocks Na+ channels (Class I), has beta-blocking properties (Class II), and blocks Ca2+ channels (Class IV). Its long half-life (~50 days) means side effects can persist for months after discontinuation. Thyroid function tests and PFTs should be monitored annually.

**Q:** What receptor mediates sympathetic effects on the sinoatrial node, and what is the physiological effect? What about parasympathetic effects?

**A:** Sympathetic: β1 receptors → increased heart rate (chronotropy). Parasympathetic: M (muscarinic) receptors → decreased conduction (negative chronotropy/dromotropy).

The autonomic dual innervation of the heart allows precise control of heart rate and conduction. β1-blockers reduce HR and contractility; muscarinic antagonists (atropine) increase HR by blocking parasympathetic tone, useful in symptomatic bradycardia.

**Q:** A patient on a new anticoagulant (rivaroxaban) is concerned about QT prolongation. What does the evidence show?

**A:** Rivaroxaban does not cause significant QT interval prolongation compared to placebo, based on randomized crossover studies. It has a favorable cardiac safety profile in this regard.

QT prolongation increases risk of torsades de pointes. Unlike some anticoagulants and other cardiovascular drugs, rivaroxaban's mechanism (direct factor Xa inhibition) does not involve cardiac ion channel effects. This distinction is important when choosing anticoagulants in patients at risk for QT prolongation.

**Q:** What are the classic features, diagnostic findings, and management of acute pericarditis?

**A:** Classic: viral prodrome, anterior precordial pain, pleuritic, relieved by sitting up and leaning forward. ECG: sinus tachycardia, diffuse ST elevation, PR depression in leads I/II/III/aVF/V4-6, reciprocal PR elevation and ST depression in aVR+V1. Management: rule out MI, high-dose NSAIDs + colchicine; consult if chronic/recurrent, large effusion, or non-viral cause.

The most sensitive ECG finding in pericarditis is Spodick's sign (downsloping TP segment), followed by ST depressions, then absence of PR depressions. Diffuse (vs. regional) ST elevation and PR depression help differentiate from STEMI. Reciprocal changes in STEMI are in the opposite territory — pericarditis lacks this pattern.

**Q:** What is Beck's triad and what condition does it suggest?

**A:** Beck's triad: hypotension + elevated JVP + muffled heart sounds = cardiac tamponade. Additional findings: tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, electrical alternans on ECG, cardiomegaly on CXR.

Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial fluid accumulates under pressure, compressing cardiac chambers and reducing ventricular filling. Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in systolic BP on inspiration) is a key finding. POCUS is diagnostic. Pericardiocentesis is definitive treatment if hemodynamically unstable.

**Q:** What is Brugada syndrome and what ECG pattern is diagnostic?

**A:** Brugada syndrome: susceptibility to deadly dysrhythmias (VFib). Type 1 ECG ('Brugada sign'): coved ST segment elevation >2 mm in ≥1 of V1–V3, followed by inverted T wave (only type that is diagnostic). Syndrome requires Brugada sign PLUS one of: family history of sudden cardiac death <45 yr, arrhythmia symptoms (syncope, seizures), or documented ventricular arrhythmias.

Brugada syndrome is a channelopathy (Na+ channel mutation) associated with sudden cardiac death, often in young men at rest or during sleep. There are 3 ECG repolarization patterns in V1–V3 but only Type 1 is diagnostic. Management includes ICD implantation in high-risk patients.

**Q:** What are the ECG criteria for ventricular tachycardia (VT)?

**A:** 3 or more consecutive premature ventricular beats at rate >100 bpm with QRS >120 ms.

VT is a life-threatening arrhythmia. Sustained VT (>30 seconds) requires immediate cardioversion if hemodynamically unstable. Other dangerous ventricular arrhythmias: Torsades de pointes (twisting pattern, 160–250 bpm), ventricular flutter (smooth sine wave ~200 bpm), ventricular fibrillation (erratic, no identifiable waves).

**Q:** What are the causes of cardiogenic syncope?

**A:** Dysrhythmia, outflow obstruction (PE, pulmonary HTN), MI, valvular disease.

Cardiogenic syncope carries the highest mortality risk among syncope etiologies. Key features suggesting cardiogenic cause include sudden loss of consciousness without warning/prodrome, occurrence during exertion, and syncope in the supine position. ECG is mandatory in all syncope evaluations.

**Q:** What investigations are indicated for all patients presenting with syncope?

**A:** ECG (tachycardia, bradycardia, blocks, WPW, long QT, Brugada, RV strain, ARVD, HCM), POCT capillary blood glucose, blood work (CBC, electrolytes, BUN/Cr, VBG, troponin, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, beta-hCG, D-dimer), consider toxicology screen.

ECG is the single most important initial investigation for syncope as it can identify life-threatening arrhythmias and structural heart disease. Troponin is important to exclude MI as a cause. Beta-hCG must be checked in women of childbearing age to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

**Q:** Describe the ECG features and management of AV conduction blocks.

**A:** 1st degree: PR >200 ms, no treatment. 2nd degree Mobitz I: progressively prolonging PR then dropped QRS (Wenckebach), usually benign. Mobitz II: fixed PR with dropped QRS, can progress to 3rd degree — needs pacemaker. 3rd degree: P waves unrelated to QRS (PP and RR intervals regular but independent), treat with atropine + transcutaneous/transvenous pacing if unstable; long-term pacemaker.

Mobitz II and complete heart block carry significant risk of progression to hemodynamic compromise and cardiac arrest. Atropine is used with caution in Mobitz II and 3rd degree block as it may paradoxically worsen AV conduction. Dopamine and epinephrine IV are alternatives if pacing unavailable.

**Q:** What is the emergency management of AVRT/AVNRT (paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia)?

**A:** 1. Vagal maneuvers (carotid massage, modified Valsalva — have patient blow into 10 cc syringe at 40 mmHg for 15 s, then lay flat with legs raised 45° for 15 s). 2. Adenosine 6 mg IV push; if no conversion, 12 mg; can repeat 12 mg once. 3. Electrical cardioversion if adenosine fails.

Modified Valsalva maneuver is effective in up to 43% of SVT cases. Adenosine blocks AV nodal conduction transiently, interrupting the reentrant circuit. Warn patients about side effects (chest pain, nausea, flushing). Continuous 12-lead ECG during maneuvers helps identify underlying rhythm and etiology.

**Q:** What are the causes of atrial fibrillation (the PIRATES mnemonic)?

**A:** P — Pulmonary (PE, COPD); I — Ischaemia/Infarction; R — Rheumatic/valvular disease; A — Anemia; T — Thyroid (hyperthyroidism); E — EtOH, Elevated blood pressure; S — Sick sinus, Stress (surgery, sepsis). Also: Cardiomyopathy.

AFib is the most common sustained dysrhythmia and decreases cardiac output by 20–30% due to loss of organized atrial contraction. Identifying and treating the underlying cause is a key treatment principle alongside stroke prevention and symptom management.

**Q:** When is it safe to cardiovert atrial fibrillation without transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)?

**A:** Safe to cardiovert if: >3 weeks of adequate anticoagulation; OR <3 weeks of adequate anticoagulation with no history of TIA/stroke, no valvular heart disease, AND one of: onset <12 h, or onset 12–48 h with CHADS2 <2.

Cardioversion carries risk of thromboembolism if a clot has formed in the left atrial appendage. TEE can exclude thrombus when anticoagulation criteria are not met. If cardioversion cannot be done safely, start appropriate anticoagulation and arrange TEE. Electrical cardioversion uses synchronized cardioversion; chemical options include procainamide, flecainide, propafenone.

**Q:** Why are AV-nodal blocking agents dangerous in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

**A:** AV-nodal blocking agents (adenosine, digoxin, diltiazem, verapamil, beta-blockers) block the AV node and preferentially conduct impulses down the accessory bypass tract at very rapid rates, leading to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Use procainamide or direct cardioversion instead.

In WPW with AFib, the accessory pathway allows antegrade conduction at rates that can trigger VFib. This is a potentially lethal interaction. Procainamide slows conduction in the accessory pathway. Recognition of a delta wave and wide-complex irregular tachycardia in AFib should prompt avoidance of all AV-nodal blocking agents.

**Q:** What is torsades de pointes and how is it treated?

**A:** A form of polymorphic VTach with QRS 'rotating around the baseline' (changing axis and amplitude — twisted ribbon appearance), associated with prolonged QT. Causes: drugs (quinidine, TCAs, erythromycin, quinolones), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, congenital long QT. Treatment: IV magnesium, temporary overdrive pacing, isoproterenol, correct underlying cause.

Prolonged QT prolongs phase 3 repolarization, creating conditions for early afterdepolarizations and reentrant arrhythmias. IV magnesium sulfate is first-line even in patients with normal Mg levels. Overdrive pacing shortens the QT interval. Avoid antiarrhythmics that further prolong QT.

**Q:** What did the REDUCE-IT trial show about icosapent ethyl (omega-3 fatty acid) for hypertriglyceridemia in patients on statins?

**A:** Icosapent ethyl (2 g BID) in patients with elevated triglycerides (1.52-5.63 mmol/L) on statin therapy significantly reduced the composite primary endpoint (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, unstable angina) by 25% relative risk (17.2% vs. 22.0%, HR 0.75). It was associated with significantly higher rates of atrial fibrillation/flutter (3.1% vs. 2.1%).

REDUCE-IT (n=8,179) established icosapent ethyl as a CV risk-reducing therapy for patients with residual hypertriglyceridemia on statin therapy. The AF risk is an important adverse effect to counsel patients about. Regular omega-3 supplements (EPA+DHA) did not show the same benefit in other trials.

## Hypertension

**Q:** What are the Hypertension Canada diagnostic thresholds for hypertension by measurement method?

**A:** Office BP ≥140/90 (≥2 visits); ABPM 24h average ≥130/80; home BP ≥135/85; AOBP ≥135/85

Hypertension Canada 2020 recommends AOBP as preferred measurement. ABPM is gold standard for white coat and masked hypertension. Single-visit diagnosis allowed if BP ≥180/110.

**Q:** What are BP targets per Hypertension Canada for general adults vs. high-risk patients?

**A:** General: <140/90 mmHg; high-risk (diabetes, CKD, CVD, Framingham risk >15%): <130/80 mmHg

SPRINT trial evidence supports lower targets for high-risk patients. Canadian guidelines adopt <130/80 for high-risk as balance between benefit and risk of adverse events.

**Q:** A 55-year-old Black man has BP 158/95 on three visits. No comorbidities. First-line antihypertensive?

**A:** Long-acting DHP-CCB (amlodipine) or thiazide diuretic (indapamide or HCTZ) — ACEi less effective as monotherapy in Black patients

Black patients have lower renin activity, so CCBs and thiazide diuretics are preferred. ACEi/ARB are still important if diabetes or CKD present. Combination therapy often required.

**Q:** A 62-year-old with HTN, type 2 diabetes, and microalbuminuria (ACR 45 mg/mmol). Preferred antihypertensive?

**A:** ACE inhibitor (e.g., ramipril) or ARB — nephroprotective via reducing intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria

ACEi/ARB are first-line for HTN with diabetes and microalbuminuria per Hypertension Canada and CDA guidelines. SGLT2 inhibitors also recommended for cardiorenal protection in diabetic CKD.

**Q:** Define hypertensive emergency and urgency.

**A:** Emergency: BP >180/120 with acute target organ damage (encephalopathy, HF, stroke, AKI, aortic dissection); Urgency: BP >180/120 without target organ damage

Hypertensive emergency requires IV treatment and BP reduction by 20-25% in first hour (not to normal — risk of ischemic stroke). Urgency managed with oral agents and close follow-up.

**Q:** A patient has BP 220/130, severe headache, papilledema, and confusion. How rapidly should BP be lowered?

**A:** Reduce MAP by 20-25% in first hour with IV labetalol or nicardipine — do NOT normalize BP rapidly

Rapid normalization causes watershed ischemia as cerebral autoregulation is shifted. Target: reduce MAP by 10-15% in 30-60 min, then to 160/100 over 2-6 hours. CT head to exclude hemorrhagic stroke.

**Q:** What secondary causes of hypertension should be investigated in a young patient with resistant HTN?

**A:** Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, sleep apnea, drugs (NSAIDs, OCP)

Secondary HTN is more common in young patients or with clinical clues. Primary hyperaldosteronism is the most common secondary cause (5-10% of all HTN). Hypertension Canada recommends secondary workup for resistant HTN.

**Q:** How is resistant hypertension defined and what is the best add-on agent?

**A:** BP ≥140/90 despite ≥3 agents at maximum doses including a diuretic; add spironolactone as 4th agent (PATHWAY-2 trial evidence)

PATHWAY-2 showed spironolactone is most effective add-on for resistant HTN. Confirm adherence, rule out white coat HTN (ABPM), and eliminate drug interactions before diagnosing true resistance.

**Q:** What lifestyle modifications reduce BP in hypertension?

**A:** DASH diet, sodium <2000 mg/day, weight loss, aerobic exercise 30-60 min 4-7 days/week, limit alcohol ≤2 drinks/day, smoking cessation

Hypertension Canada quantifies benefit: DASH diet ~11 mmHg, sodium restriction ~5 mmHg, weight loss ~1 mmHg/kg, exercise ~4-9 mmHg. Lifestyle changes can achieve targets without medication in stage 1 HTN.

**Q:** A 70-year-old has isolated systolic hypertension (BP 168/72). Preferred antihypertensive?

**A:** Long-acting DHP-CCB (amlodipine) or thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) — most evidence for isolated systolic HTN in elderly

SHEP and Syst-Eur trials demonstrated benefit of treating isolated systolic HTN. Target SBP <140 in elderly. Slow titration to avoid postural hypotension.

**Q:** What causes ACE inhibitor cough and what is the alternative?

**A:** ACEi cough from bradykinin accumulation; switch to ARB which does not affect bradykinin metabolism

ACEi cough occurs in 5-20% (more common in Asians, women, non-smokers). Class effect — switching to another ACEi will not help. ACEi and ARBs should not be combined due to AKI and hyperkalemia risk.

**Q:** What antihypertensives are safe in pregnancy?

**A:** Labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine XL are safe; avoid ACEi and ARBs (teratogenic — fetal renal agenesis, oligohydramnios)

SOGC guidelines recommend treatment for BP ≥140/90 in pregnancy. Severe HTN (≥160/110) requires urgent treatment to prevent maternal stroke. Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia.

**Q:** What is the CV risk reduction from antihypertensive therapy?

**A:** Each 10 mmHg reduction in SBP reduces stroke risk ~35-40%, MI risk ~20-25%, heart failure ~50%

Meta-analyses confirm significant CV benefit from BP lowering regardless of drug class, proportional to degree of reduction. Absolute risk reduction depends on baseline risk.

**Q:** A 45-year-old has BP 152/96 and 10-year CV risk of 18%. When should pharmacotherapy start?

**A:** Treat when BP ≥130/80 for high-risk patients (10-year CV risk ≥15%); lifestyle modification accompanies pharmacotherapy

Hypertension Canada 2020 incorporates global CV risk. For high-risk patients, treatment threshold is lower and target is <130/80 mmHg, based on SPRINT evidence.

**Q:** What is the role of beta-blockers in hypertension per Hypertension Canada?

**A:** NOT first-line for uncomplicated HTN in patients ≥60 years; preferred for compelling indications: post-MI, HFrEF, angina, AF rate control

Hypertension Canada downgraded beta-blockers due to inferior stroke prevention in elderly (LIFE trial). Acceptable option in patients <60 without compelling indication.

**Q:** A patient on amlodipine 10mg and ramipril 10mg has BP 148/94. Next step?

**A:** Add thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide SR 1.5mg or HCTZ 25mg) — triple therapy ACEi + CCB + diuretic

Hypertension Canada recommends ACEi + CCB + diuretic as the preferred triple regimen. Three-drug combination more effective than any dual combination.

**Q:** What BP target and preferred agents for CKD without diabetes?

**A:** Target <140/90; ACEi or ARB for nephroprotection — avoid combining ACEi + ARB

ACEi/ARB recommended for CKD with proteinuria (ACR >30 mg/mmol) to reduce intraglomerular pressure. Up to 30% creatinine rise acceptable if K+ remains <5.5 mEq/L.

**Q:** A hypertensive patient has hypokalemia (K+ 2.9), suppressed renin, and elevated aldosterone/renin ratio. Diagnosis?

**A:** Primary hyperaldosteronism; most common cause is bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (60%) or aldosterone-producing adenoma (35%)

Screen: aldosterone/renin ratio >30 with aldosterone >15 ng/dL. Confirm with saline suppression test. CT then adrenal vein sampling to lateralize. Treatment: adenoma → adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone.

**Q:** How is pheochromocytoma diagnosed and what is the pre-operative treatment priority?

**A:** Diagnose with plasma free metanephrines or 24h urine catecholamines; pre-op: alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine), THEN beta-blockade

Plasma free metanephrines have highest sensitivity (96%). MRI/CT adrenal localizes tumor. Never start beta-blocker before alpha-blocker — risk of hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha stimulation.

**Q:** How should BP be properly measured per Hypertension Canada?

**A:** Rest 5 min, no caffeine/smoking 30 min prior, empty bladder, seated back supported, arm at heart level, appropriate cuff size, average 2-3 readings — prefer AOBP

AOBP eliminates white-coat effect. AOBP measures 5 consecutive readings while patient is alone; mean of readings 2-5 is used. Measurement errors are a common cause of apparent treatment failure.

**Q:** A 38-year-old woman presents with severe headache, BP 230/135 mmHg, confusion, and bilateral papilledema. Creatinine is 2.8 (baseline unknown). Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red cell casts. Her Hgb is 7.8 g/dL with schistocytes on peripheral smear. What is this condition and what is the immediate management?

A) Hypertensive emergency with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — IV labetalol, target 25% MAP reduction in first hour
B) Malignant hypertension — immediate reversal to normal BP to prevent permanent renal failure
C) Hypertensive urgency — oral antihypertensives over 24–48 hours
D) Eclampsia — magnesium sulfate and delivery

**A:** A) Hypertensive emergency with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — IV labetalol, target 25% MAP reduction in first hour

Hypertensive emergency with target organ damage (encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia/TMA) requires immediate IV antihypertensive therapy. Key principle: reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour (to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion — risk of ischemic stroke, watershed infarcts). Over 2–6 hours, reduce to 160/100, then normalize over 24–48 hours. IV labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine are first-line. Nitroprusside for truly refractory cases. The schistocytes + renal failure + severe hypertension = hypertensive TMA (malignant hypertension-associated TMA) — distinct from TTP/HUS but treated by BP control.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man with resistant hypertension (BP 162/98 on 3 drugs including a diuretic at maximum tolerated doses) undergoes workup. Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) is 38 (elevated, > 30). CT adrenal shows a 1.8cm left adrenal adenoma. What is the next diagnostic step before treatment?

A) Start spironolactone — the adenoma is the culprit
B) Proceed directly to laparoscopic left adrenalectomy — CT is diagnostic
C) Adrenal vein sampling (AVS) to confirm lateralization
D) 24-hour urine free cortisol to exclude Cushing's syndrome

**A:** C) Adrenal vein sampling (AVS) to confirm lateralization

CT adrenal has poor sensitivity/specificity for diagnosing primary aldosteronism (PA) lateralization — CT can miss microadenomas, misattribute bilateral PA to a visible incidentaloma, or identify non-functional adenomas. Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS) is the gold standard to confirm lateralization BEFORE surgery. AVS compares aldosterone-to-cortisol ratio in left vs. right adrenal vein — lateralization ratio >4:1 (with ACTH stimulation) confirms unilateral disease → adrenalectomy. Bilateral disease → spironolactone/eplerenone. Proceeding to surgery based on CT alone misclassifies up to 37% of patients (Endocrine Society guidelines — AVS mandatory before surgery).

**Q:** A 32-year-old woman presents with uncontrolled hypertension, headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. 24-hour urine shows elevated metanephrines (4x upper limit of normal) and normetanephrines (3x upper limit of normal).
