BP is 185/110 on amlodipine 10mg and lisinopril 10mg. CT shows a 3cm right adrenal mass. What is the FIRST medication to add before surgery?

A) IV phentolamine — immediate alpha blockade for the hypertensive crisis
B) Oral phenoxybenzamine — non-selective alpha-blockade for 10–14 days pre-op
C) Propranolol — beta-blockade to control heart rate
D) Metyrosine — catecholamine synthesis inhibitor to reduce tumor secretion

**A:** B) Oral phenoxybenzamine — non-selective alpha-blockade for 10–14 days pre-op

Pheochromocytoma management pre-operatively: (1) Alpha-blockade FIRST (10–14 days) with phenoxybenzamine (irreversible non-selective) or doxazosin (selective alpha-1). This is mandatory before surgery to prevent hypertensive crisis during tumor manipulation. (2) THEN add beta-blockade (propranolol) — never give beta-blockers first (unopposed alpha stimulation → severe hypertension). (3) Salt and fluid loading to correct volume depletion from chronic vasoconstriction. (4) Surgery (laparoscopic adrenalectomy) after adequate alpha blockade confirmed (target BP < 130/80, mild orthostatic drop). Phentolamine IV is for acute crisis management.

**Q:** A 55-year-old Black man has stage 2 hypertension (BP 158/96) with no diabetes and no proteinuria. His creatinine is normal. Which first-line antihypertensive class is most appropriate as initial monotherapy based on current evidence and guidelines?

A) ACE inhibitor — superior cardiovascular protection in all patient groups
B) Thiazide diuretic or calcium channel blocker
C) Beta-blocker — preferred for its sympatholytic effects in high-renin hypertension
D) ARB — equivalent to ACE inhibitor without cough risk

**A:** B) Thiazide diuretic or calcium channel blocker

Black patients have lower renin activity and respond less well to renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) as monotherapy — these agents have lower antihypertensive efficacy and reduced HF/stroke prevention efficacy in this population when used as single agents. The ALLHAT trial confirmed thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone) and CCBs are superior in reducing BP and cardiovascular outcomes in Black patients with stage 2 HTN. ACE inhibitors as monotherapy are also associated with higher rates of angioedema in Black patients. CCBs and thiazides are first-line in guidelines (JNC 8, NICE, Hypertension Canada) for Black patients.

**Q:** A 62-year-old woman with hypertension is started on hydrochlorothiazide 25mg. Two months later, BP is controlled but her fasting glucose is 6.8 mmol/L (previously 5.6), Na+ is 131 mEq/L, K+ is 3.1 mEq/L. Which thiazide-related metabolic adverse effect is MOST clinically significant in a patient with pre-diabetes?

A) Hyponatremia — directly increases risk of osmotic demyelination
B) New-onset diabetes mellitus — thiazides worsen insulin resistance
C) Hypokalemia — increases risk of arrhythmias
D) Hyperuricemia — increases risk of gout

**A:** B) New-onset diabetes mellitus — thiazides worsen insulin resistance

Thiazide diuretics cause a constellation of metabolic effects: hypokalemia (which itself worsens insulin resistance and impairs beta-cell insulin secretion), hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, and hyperlipidemia. In a pre-diabetic patient, the progression to new-onset diabetes is the most clinically significant long-term complication — new-onset diabetes associated with antihypertensives carries the same cardiovascular risk as pre-existing diabetes (ALLHAT, VALUE trials). In this patient, considering switching to a CCB or ACE inhibitor + potassium repletion is prudent. Chlorthalidone (more potent, longer half-life) has superior CV outcomes but causes more metabolic derangements than HCTZ.

**Q:** How is hypertension diagnosed per Hypertension Canada?

**A:** Office BP >=140/90 on >=2 visits OR >=130/85 on office then confirmed with out-of-office measurement: ABPM daytime mean >=135/85 or HBPM mean >=135/85. ABPM is gold standard (rules out white coat HTN)

Hypertension Canada 2020. Automated office BP (AOBP) preferred over manual. White coat HTN (elevated office, normal out-of-office): 15-30%, monitor but may not need treatment. Masked HTN (normal office, elevated out-of-office): treat as hypertensive. Home BP lower thresholds than office.

**Q:** What are the first-line antihypertensive drug classes and how are they selected?

**A:** First-line: ACEi/ARB, thiazide/thiazide-like (chlorthalidone preferred), long-acting DHP-CCB (amlodipine). With diabetes/CKD+proteinuria: ACEi/ARB mandatory. Black patients: CCB or thiazide first. Young white: ACEi/ARB

Hypertension Canada. Most patients need >=2 drugs. Single pill combinations improve adherence. Target: <140/90 general, <130/80 diabetes. Do NOT combine ACEi+ARB. Beta-blockers not first-line for uncomplicated HTN (inferior stroke prevention). Thiazide-like (chlorthalidone, indapamide) preferred over HCTZ.

**Q:** What is the workup for resistant hypertension?

**A:** Definition: BP above target despite 3 drugs at optimal doses including a diuretic. Confirm: rule out non-adherence (most common), white coat effect (ABPM), secondary causes. Workup: aldosterone/renin ratio, renal artery doppler, catecholamines, cortisol, TSH, sleep study

Secondary HTN causes: primary aldosteronism (most common, ARR screening), renal artery stenosis (young female=FMD, older=atherosclerotic), pheochromocytoma (episodic), Cushing, OSA, coarctation, thyroid. Fourth-line drug: spironolactone 25-50mg (PATHWAY-2 trial).

**Q:** What is primary aldosteronism and how is it screened and diagnosed?

**A:** Screening: aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR). Positive: ARR>100 pmol/L per ng/mL/h AND aldosterone >416 pmol/L. Confirm with salt loading or fludrocortisone suppression test. Subtype: CT adrenals + adrenal vein sampling. Treat: unilateral adenoma=surgery, bilateral=spironolactone

Most common cause of secondary HTN (5-10% of all HTN, up to 20% of resistant). Screen: resistant HTN, hypokalemia, adrenal incidentaloma, early-onset HTN, FHx. Hold interfering drugs: spironolactone 6wk, ACEi/ARB 2wk before testing (though practically difficult).

**Q:** How is hypertensive urgency vs emergency managed?

**A:** Urgency: severe HTN (>=180/120) WITHOUT end-organ damage. Manage: oral agents (captopril, clonidine, amlodipine), lower BP over 24-48h in outpatient setting. Emergency: severe HTN WITH end-organ damage (encephalopathy, ACS, aortic dissection, eclampsia, acute HF, papilledema). IV agents in ICU

Hypertensive emergency IV agents: labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin (ACS/HF), nitroprusside (aortic dissection, but cyanide risk). Target: 25% reduction in first hour, then to 160/100 over next 2-6h. Exception: aortic dissection (SBP<120 in 20min) and stroke (permissive HTN unless >220/120 or tPA candidate).

**Q:** How is hypertension managed in pregnancy?

**A:** Chronic HTN: target <140/90. Drugs: labetalol (first-line), nifedipine XL, methyldopa. AVOID: ACEi/ARB (teratogenic), atenolol (IUGR). Preeclampsia prevention: ASA 162mg from 12wk if high-risk. Severe HTN (>=160/110): urgent IV labetalol or PO nifedipine

Preeclampsia: HTN + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after 20wk. Severe features: SBP>=160, thrombocytopenia, liver dysfunction, renal, pulmonary edema, visual/cerebral. Definitive treatment: delivery. Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis. CHIPS trial: tight vs less-tight control both acceptable.

**Q:** What lifestyle modifications reduce blood pressure?

**A:** DASH diet: 8-14 mmHg reduction. Sodium restriction <2000mg/d: 2-8 mmHg. Weight loss: 1 mmHg per kg lost. Exercise 30-60min 4-7d/wk: 4-9 mmHg. Alcohol reduction: 2-4 mmHg. Smoking cessation: reduces CV risk but minimal direct BP effect

Hypertension Canada recommends lifestyle as first-line for stage 1 HTN without target organ damage. Combination of interventions is additive. DASH diet: rich in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, reduced saturated fat. Potassium supplementation beneficial if not on ACEi/ARB.

**Q:** What are the target organ damages of hypertension?

**A:** Brain: stroke, TIA, hypertensive encephalopathy, vascular dementia. Heart: LVH, HF, CAD, AF. Kidney: CKD, proteinuria, hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Eye: hypertensive retinopathy (AV nicking, cotton-wool spots, flame hemorrhages, papilledema). Aorta: dissection, aneurysm

Screen for TOD in all hypertensives: ECG (LVH), urine ACR (proteinuria), creatinine (CKD), fundoscopy if severe/emergency. LVH on echo is stronger predictor than ECG. Regression of LVH with treatment improves prognosis. ACEi/ARB are nephroprotective in proteinuric CKD.

**Q:** What are the side effects of common antihypertensives?

**A:** ACEi: cough (10-15%), angioedema (rare), hyperkalemia, AKI. ARB: similar but no cough. Thiazide: hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia. CCB (DHP): edema, headache, flushing. Beta-blocker: fatigue, bradycardia, bronchospasm, masking hypoglycemia

ACEi cough: switch to ARB. Angioedema: do NOT switch to ARB (small cross-reactivity). Thiazide hypokalemia: add K+ supplement or switch to K-sparing. DHP CCB edema: not improved by diuretics (arteriolar, not volume). Combination ACEi+CCB reduces edema.

**Q:** When should pheochromocytoma be suspected and how is it diagnosed?

**A:** Suspect: paroxysmal HTN, headache, diaphoresis, palpitations (classic triad), resistant HTN, adrenal incidentaloma, family history (MEN2, VHL, NF1). Diagnosis: plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive) or 24h urine catecholamines/metanephrines. Imaging: CT/MRI after biochemical confirmation

Pheo is rare but potentially lethal if undiagnosed (hypertensive crisis during surgery/anesthesia). Rule of 10s: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% malignant, 30% familial. Pre-operative preparation: alpha-blocker first (phenoxybenzamine/doxazosin) then add beta-blocker. NEVER beta-block first (unopposed alpha crisis).

**Q:** What are the causes of secondary hypertension and when to suspect them?

**A:** Young onset (<30), resistant HTN, sudden onset, hypokalemia (hyperaldo), renal bruits (renovascular), truncal obesity/striae (Cushing), paroxysmal HTN/palpitations (pheochromocytoma)

Workup: renin/aldosterone ratio (hyperaldo), renal US Doppler (renovascular), 24h urine catecholamines (pheo), overnight dex suppression (Cushing), sleep study (OSA). Most common secondary cause: renal parenchymal disease.

**Q:** What defines resistant hypertension and how is it managed?

**A:** BP above target despite 3 agents at optimal doses (including a diuretic). Confirm with 24h ABPM. Rule out pseudoresistance (non-adherence, white coat) and secondary causes

Hypertension Canada: add spironolactone as 4th agent (PATHWAY-2 trial). Consider renal denervation in select patients. Device-based therapy emerging. Ensure adequate diuretic dosing (chlorthalidone preferred).

**Q:** What are the Hypertension Canada 2020 BP targets?

**A:** Standard risk: <140/90. High risk (diabetes, CKD, high CV risk): <130/80. SPRINT-eligible (high CV risk, no diabetes): <120 systolic (automated office BP)

Measure with automated office BP (AOBP) — lower thresholds than manual. Home BP: average >=135/85 = HTN. 24h ABPM: daytime >=135/85 or 24h >=130/80 = HTN.

**Q:** What is the first-line antihypertensive selection based on comorbidities?

**A:** ACEi/ARB: diabetes, CKD, proteinuria, HF. CCB: isolated systolic HTN, Black patients. Thiazide: uncomplicated HTN, elderly. Beta-blocker: recent MI, HFrEF, rate control

Hypertension Canada recommends any of ACEi/ARB, CCB, or thiazide for uncomplicated. Avoid ACEi+ARB combo. Beta-blockers NOT first-line unless specific indication. SGLT2i additive benefit in diabetic HTN.

**Q:** What distinguishes hypertensive emergency from urgency?

**A:** Emergency: BP >180/120 WITH acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, AKI, aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, retinal hemorrhage). Urgency: severely elevated BP WITHOUT end-organ damage

Emergency: IV antihypertensives (labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside), ICU, reduce MAP 25% in first hour. Urgency: oral agents, reduce over 24-48h. Aortic dissection target HR<60, SBP<120 with IV esmolol+nitroprusside.

**Q:** What is white coat hypertension and how is it confirmed?

**A:** Office BP elevated but normal out-of-office (ABPM daytime <135/85 or home BP <135/85). Prevalence 15-30% of diagnosed HTN. Lower CV risk than sustained HTN but higher than normotension

Hypertension Canada: confirm HTN diagnosis with ABPM or home BP monitoring in most patients. Masked HTN is opposite: normal office, elevated out-of-office — higher risk, often underdiagnosed.

**Q:** What distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from a hypertensive urgency?

**A:** Hypertensive emergency: severely elevated BP (often >180/120) WITH acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, AKI, aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, eclampsia). Requires IV antihypertensives in ICU with goal to reduce MAP by 20-25% in the first hour. Hypertensive urgency: severely elevated BP WITHOUT end-organ damage; treat with oral agents.

The critical distinction is end-organ damage, not a specific BP threshold. Hypertension Canada guidelines emphasize that overly rapid BP reduction can cause watershed ischemia. Exceptions: aortic dissection targets SBP <120 in 20 minutes.

**Q:** List the key investigations to assess end-organ damage in a hypertensive emergency.

**A:** Fundoscopy (retinopathy, papilledema), ECG (LVH, ischemia), troponin, CBC with smear (MAHA), creatinine/BUN, urinalysis (proteinuria, hematuria, casts), electrolytes, chest X-ray (pulmonary edema, widened mediastinum), CT head if neurological symptoms.

End-organ damage assessment must be systematic and rapid. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes) indicates malignant hypertension. Hypertension Canada emphasizes fundoscopy as a bedside tool often underutilized in acute settings.

**Q:** A 35-year-old woman has office BP 150/95 but home BP averaging 125/80. What is the diagnosis and management?

**A:** White coat hypertension. Confirm with 24-hour ABPM: if daytime average <135/85 and 24-hour average <130/80, no pharmacotherapy needed. Monitor annually as 30-40% progress to sustained HTN.

Hypertension Canada defines white coat HTN as elevated office BP with normal out-of-office BP confirmed by ABPM or home BP monitoring. These patients have lower cardiovascular risk than sustained HTN but higher risk than normotensives.

**Q:** What is masked hypertension and why is it clinically significant?

**A:** Normal office BP (<140/90) but elevated out-of-office BP (home >=135/85 or 24-hour ABPM >=130/80). Carries cardiovascular risk equivalent to sustained hypertension and is often undiagnosed, affecting 10-15% of the population.

Masked HTN is associated with increased LVH, carotid intima-media thickness, and cardiovascular events. Hypertension Canada recommends considering ABPM in patients with normal office BP but evidence of target organ damage. Treatment is indicated when confirmed.

**Q:** A 28-year-old with refractory hypertension, hypokalemia, and abdominal bruit. Most likely diagnosis and workup?

**A:** Renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). Workup: CTA or MRA of renal arteries (string-of-beads appearance), plasma renin and aldosterone, duplex ultrasonography as alternative screening.

FMD is the most common cause of renovascular HTN in young women. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis predominates in older patients. Hypertension Canada recommends imaging when clinical suspicion exists. Percutaneous angioplasty is first-line for FMD.

**Q:** Which IV antihypertensive is preferred for hypertensive emergency with acute aortic dissection?

**A:** IV esmolol first-line to reduce HR to <60 bpm and SBP to <120 mmHg within 20 minutes. If BP remains elevated after adequate HR control, add IV nicardipine or nitroprusside. Never use vasodilators alone (reflex tachycardia worsens dissection).

Beta-blockade must precede vasodilation to prevent reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt. Labetalol is an acceptable alternative. CCS guidelines emphasize urgent surgical consultation for Type A dissection.

**Q:** What are Hypertension Canada's recommended first-line agents for uncomplicated essential hypertension?

**A:** Thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide preferred over HCTZ), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or long-acting dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine). Beta-blockers are NOT first-line for uncomplicated HTN in patients >=60 years.

Hypertension Canada 2020 guidelines specifically recommend thiazide-like diuretics over HCTZ due to superior outcome data. Single-pill combinations are encouraged when BP is >20/10 above target. ACEi/ARB combination is contraindicated per ONTARGET trial.

**Q:** A patient with CKD (eGFR 35) and proteinuria has BP 155/95. What is the target BP and preferred agent?

**A:** Target BP <130/80. ACEi or ARB first-line to reduce proteinuria and slow CKD progression. Tolerate up to 30% rise in creatinine. Add loop diuretic (preferred when eGFR <30) if needed.

Hypertension Canada recommends ACEi/ARB for hypertensive CKD with proteinuria (ACR >30 mg/mmol). REIN and RENAAL trials demonstrated renoprotective benefits independent of BP lowering. Never combine ACEi + ARB.

**Q:** What is Hypertension Canada's recommended algorithm for diagnosing hypertension?

**A:** If office BP >=180/110, diagnose immediately. If 140-179/90-109, confirm with out-of-office measurement: ABPM preferred (daytime >=135/85 or 24-hour >=130/80 confirms HTN), or home BP series (duplicate morning/evening readings for 7 days, discard first day).

Hypertension Canada emphasizes out-of-office BP measurement to avoid treating white coat HTN. ABPM is the gold standard and detects masked HTN and nocturnal patterns. Automated office BP (AOBP) with patient resting alone is preferred in-office method.

**Q:** A patient on 3 antihypertensives including a diuretic at optimal doses still has BP 160/100. What secondary causes should be investigated?

**A:** Primary aldosteronism (aldosterone-to-renin ratio), renal artery stenosis (CTA/MRA), pheochromocytoma (24-hour urine metanephrines), Cushing syndrome (overnight dexamethasone suppression), obstructive sleep apnea (polysomnography), thyroid disease.

Resistant hypertension affects 10-15% of treated hypertensives. Primary aldosteronism prevalence is 8-20% in this group. Hypertension Canada recommends screening for secondary causes and confirming adherence. Spironolactone is effective add-on therapy per the PATHWAY-2 trial.

**Q:** What alternative exists for patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors?

**A:** ARBs (Angiotensin Receptor Blockers)

ARBs provide similar cardiovascular protection by blocking the renin-angiotensin system at the receptor level.

**Q:** Why is irreversible pulmonary hypertension a contraindication to cardiac transplantation?

**A:** The donor heart is denervated and cannot compensate for increased pulmonary vascular resistance; it will fail in the presence of fixed pulmonary hypertension

Without the ability to increase cardiac output through sympathetic stimulation, a transplanted heart cannot overcome elevated pulmonary pressures.

**Q:** What are the alpha-2 agonist drugs and their uses?

**A:** Clonidine, methyldopa - used for hypertension (centrally acting), sedation

Alpha-2 agonists act centrally to reduce sympathetic outflow, lowering blood pressure. Methyldopa is safe in pregnancy.

**Q:** What is clonidine's mechanism and use?

**A:** Alpha-2 agonist used for hypertension and pain management

Clonidine stimulates central alpha-2 receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow and causing hypotension. Also used as an adjunct for chronic pain.

**Q:** What is the mechanism of prazosin?

**A:** Selective alpha-1 antagonist used for hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia

Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors, causing vasodilation and reducing peripheral vascular resistance. First-dose hypotension is a known adverse effect.

**Q:** What conditions are associated with porphyria cutanea tarda?

**A:** Hemochromatosis, alcohol abuse, diabetes mellitus, estrogen therapy, NSAIDs, HIV, hepatitis C, increased iron indices - all cause uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency

Multiple factors can inhibit the enzyme responsible for heme synthesis, leading to accumulation of porphyrins that deposit in the skin and cause photosensitivity.

**Q:** What enzyme deficiency causes Porphyria Cutanea Tarda?

**A:** Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency leads to excess heme precursors (uroporphyrins).

This enzyme normally converts uroporphyrinogen to coproporphyrinogen; its deficiency causes porphyrin accumulation and photosensitivity.

**Q:** What causes the photosensitivity in Porphyria Cutanea Tarda?

**A:** Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency leads to excess heme precursors (uroporphyrins) that absorb UV light and generate reactive oxygen species in the skin

Porphyrins act as photosensitizers; their accumulation in the skin causes phototoxic reactions, particularly in sun-exposed areas

**Q:** What are the three types of lice and their typical locations?

**A:** Phthirus pubis (pubic lice), Pediculus humanus capitis (scalp lice), Pediculus humanus humanus (body lice). Each attaches to its respective body hair and feeds on the nearby body site.

Lice are species-specific寄生虫. Identifying the type helps determine transmission route and treatment approach.

**Q:** What are the treatment options for unresectable or metastatic melanoma?

**A:** Anti-CTLA-4 agents (ipilimumab), anti-PD1 agents (nivolumab, pembrolizumab), high-dose IFN, chemotherapy (dacarbazine), and BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib) for BRAF V600E mutations

Metastatic melanoma treatment includes immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy for BRAF-mutated tumors, with radiotherapy as adjunctive treatment.

**Q:** What is the maximum duration of cyclosporine therapy and why?

**A:** Maximum 2 years due to long-term effects including nephrotoxicity and hypertension

Cyclosporine 2.5-4mg/kg/d is used for psoriasis, lichen planus, and recalcitrant urticaria. Long-term effects preclude use beyond 2 years; earlier discontinuation is preferred when possible.

**Q:** Why must isotretinoin be stopped before tetracycline antibiotics?

**A:** Both drug classes can cause pseudotumor cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension)

Concurrent use of isotretinoin and tetracyclines increases the risk of pseudotumor cerebri. Minocycline and doxycycline should be discontinued before starting isotretinoin.

**Q:** What are the first-line treatment options for unresectable or metastatic melanoma?

**A:** Anti-CTLA-4 agents (ipilimumab), anti-PD1 agents (nivolumab, pembrolizumab), high-dose IFN, and chemotherapy (dacarbazine)

Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors is the mainstay of treatment for advanced melanoma, with combination therapy often used for better response rates.

**Q:** When is bicarbonate indicated in DKA?

**A:** Only when patient is at risk of shock or death (typically pH <7.0)

Bicarbonate is not routinely given in DKA due to risk of paradoxical acidosis, hypokalemia, and cerebral edema; it is reserved for severe acidemia with hemodynamic compromise.

**Q:** What are the expected pH and bicarbonate values in HHS?

**A:** pH >7.3 and bicarbonate >18 mEq/L

Unlike DKA, HHS lacks significant metabolic acidosis; these values help distinguish between the two hyperglycemic emergencies.

**Q:** When is bicarbonate therapy indicated in DKA?

**A:** Bicarbonate is not given unless patient is at risk of shock or death (typically pH <7.0).

Routine bicarbonate use in DKA is avoided as it can cause paradoxical CNS acidosis and hypokalemia.

**Q:** What are the expected pH and bicarbonate values in HHS (vs DKA)?

**A:** pH >7.3 and bicarbonate >18 mEq/L (in contrast to DKA which has acidosis).

HHS lacks significant ketoacidosis, which differentiates it from DKA.

**Q:** What is the lag time for pneumonitis after hydrocarbon ingestion or smoke inhalation?

**A:** 6-8 hours

Pneumonitis may not be immediately apparent; observation and repeated examination are required

**Q:** When should bicarbonate be given in DKA?

**A:** Only when patient is at risk of shock or death (typically pH <7.0)

Bicarbonate is not routinely given in DKA; it is reserved for severe acidemia with hemodynamic compromise.

**Q:** What are typical pH and bicarbonate values in HHS (not DKA)?

**A:** pH >7.3, bicarbonate >18 mEq/L

HHS lacks significant ketoacidosis, so pH and bicarbonate are preserved compared to DKA.

**Q:** Why should patients with hydrocarbon or smoke inhalation be observed for 6-8 hours?

**A:** Pneumonitis may lag 6-8 hours after ingestion/inhalation

Chemical pneumonitis from hydrocarbon aspiration can have a delayed presentation, requiring observation for clinical and radiographic changes.

**Q:** When is bicarbonate indicated in DKA management?

**A:** Bicarbonate is NOT given unless patient is at risk of shock or death, typically when pH <7.0.

Routine bicarbonate use in DKA is avoided as it can cause paradoxical acidosis and other complications.

**Q:** What causes secondary hypertriglyceridemia?

**A:** Obesity/metabolic syndrome, DM, drugs (corticosteroids, estrogen, hydrochlorothiazide, retinoic acid, beta-blockers, anti-retrovirals, antipsychotics, OCPs), alcohol, high carbohydrate/high fat diet, pregnancy

Severe hypertriglyceridemia (>10 mmol/L) increases risk of pancreatitis.

**Q:** Why should patients with hydrocarbon/smoke inhalation be observed for 6-8 hours?

**A:** Pneumonitis may lag 6-8 hours

Chemical pneumonitis from hydrocarbon aspiration may be delayed and not appear clinically or radiographically for 6-8 hours post-ingestion.

**Q:** In insulin pump therapy, how is mealtime bolus calculated?

**A:** Based on carbohydrate:insulin ratios programmed by the patient

At meals, patients program the pump to deliver insulin boluses calculated using their individual carbohydrate-to-insulin ratios.

**Q:** In DKA, what happens to serum bicarbonate?

**A:** Decreased (metabolic acidosis)

Serum HCO3- decreases in DKA due to consumption of bicarbonate by ketoacids in the setting of anion gap metabolic acidosis.

**Q:** What are the key features of insulin pump therapy (CSII)?

**A:** External device providing continuous basal rapid-acting insulin; patient programs bolus based on carb:insulin ratios; improved quality of life/flexibility; risk of DKA if disconnected

Uses rapid-acting analogues (aspart, glulisine, lispro). Coverage varies by province for T1DM.

**Q:** What is theinsulin:carbohydrate ratio used in pump therapy?

**A:** Patient programs the pump based on carbohydrate:insulin ratios

At mealtimes, patients program the insulin pump to deliver boluses based on carbohydrate intake and individualized ratios.

**Q:** What inhibits the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?

**A:** Dopamine, prostaglandins, and ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) inhibit renin release; ACE inhibitors and ARBs block the cascade

These factors reduce aldosterone production and promote natriuresis.

**Q:** What is the function of cortisol?

**A:** Glucocorticoid involved in metabolism regulation, supports blood pressure and vasomotor tone, and involved in behavioural regulation and immunosuppression

Cortisol is regulated by the HPA axis and has widespread effects on multiple organ systems.

**Q:** What medications can interfere with primary aldosteronism testing and may need to be held prior to testing?

**A:** Various antihypertensives and diuretics can interfere with screening and confirmatory tests for primary aldosteronism

Medications affecting the RAAS axis can cause false positive or negative results.

**Q:** Which drugs can cause hypercalcemia?

**A:** Thiazide diuretics, lithium, theophylline, estrogen, tamoxifen, vitamin A, excessive calcium carbonate or vitamin D supplements

Multiple drugs affect calcium homeostasis through different mechanisms - thiazides reduce calcium excretion, lithium increases PTH secretion

**Q:** What is the function of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)?

**A:** Regulates blood pressure, sodium balance, and potassium balance through angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone release

RAAS activation leads to renal Na+ retention, K+ excretion, arteriolar vasoconstriction, and promotion of ADH release.

**Q:** What BP target was considered 'intensive' in the ACCORD Blood Pressure Trial?

**A:** sBP <120 mmHg

The ACCORD BP Trial randomized T2DM patients with CV risk factors to intensive (sBP <120 mmHg) vs standard (sBP <140 mmHg) blood pressure control.

**Q:** In the ACCORD Blood Pressure trial, did intensive BP control (<120 mmHg) reduce major CV events compared to standard control (<140 mmHg)?

**A:** No significant reduction in primary outcome (major CV events), but significant reduction in any stroke (0.32%/yr vs 0.53%/yr, p=0.01)

Intensive BP lowering reduced stroke risk but did not reduce the composite major CV event rate in T2DM patients with CV risk factors.

**Q:** What was the population size in the ACCORD Blood Pressure trial?

**A:** 4733 patients with T2DM

The ACCORD BP trial enrolled 4733 patients with T2DM and CV risk factors who had systolic BP between 130-180 mmHg.

**Q:** In the ACCORD BP trial, did intensive blood pressure control (<120 mmHg) reduce major CV events in T2DM?

**A:** No - there was no significant difference in primary outcome (major CV events) between intensive and standard groups

While intensive therapy did significantly reduce any stroke (0.32%/yr vs 0.53%/yr, P=0.01) and nonfatal stroke, it did not reduce the composite major CV event rate.

**Q:** What was the mean number of antihypertensive medications at 1 year in the intensive arm of ACCORD BP?

**A:** 3.4 medications (95% CI 3.4-3.5)

This was compared to 2.1 medications (95% CI 2.1-2.2) in the standard arm, demonstrating the intensive treatment required significantly more drugs.

**Q:** What is the optimal blood pressure target for diabetics?

**A:** <130/80 mmHg

Blood pressure control in diabetics targets <130/80 to reduce cardiovascular complications.

**Q:** In the ACCORD BP Trial, did intensive blood pressure control (<120 mmHg) reduce major cardiovascular events in T2DM patients?

**A:** No, intensive BP control did not reduce major CV events, but it did significantly reduce stroke incidence (0.32%/yr vs 0.53%/yr, P=0.01)

The ACCORD BP Trial studied 4733 T2DM patients with CV risk factors comparing intensive (sBP <120 mmHg) vs standard (sBP <140 mmHg) therapy for 4.7 years

**Q:** What medications should be considered in diabetes management?

**A:** ACEI/ARB (renal protection), Statin (cardiovascular risk reduction), ASA (secondary prevention)

Diabetes patients often require cardioprotective and renoprotective medications beyond glycemic control.

**Q:** What medications are recommended in diabetes management for CV risk reduction?

**A:** Consider ACE-I/ARB, Statin, and ASA

Cardiovascular risk reduction is a key component of diabetes management.

**Q:** What is the diabetes quick reference for optimal control?

**A:** HbA1C <7%, BP <130/80, Cholesterol LDL-C <2 mmol/L if treating, consider ACEi/ARB, Statin, ASA, Exercise/Eating, Smoking Cessation

These targets represent evidence-based optimal control goals to prevent diabetes complications.

**Q:** List the key drug classes to consider in diabetes management

**A:** ACEi/ARB (for blood pressure/renal protection), Statin (for cholesterol), ASA (for cardiovascular protection)

Diabetes management includes considering ACE inhibitors or ARBs for blood pressure and renal protection, statins for cholesterol, and ASA for cardiovascular protection.

**Q:** What are the blood pressure thresholds for diagnosing hypertension in non-diabetic patients using automated office BP?

**A:** >135/85 mmHg

For non-diabetic patients, AOBP >135/85 mmHg or OBPM ≥140/90 mmHg suggests hypertension.

**Q:** What are the blood pressure thresholds for diagnosing hypertension in diabetic patients?

**A:** >130/80 mmHg

Diabetic patients have lower thresholds due to increased cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What are the ABPM thresholds for diagnosing hypertension?

**A:** Daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg

ABPM provides more accurate assessment and rules out white coat hypertension.

**Q:** What symptoms may suggest hypertension based on organ-specific effects?

**A:** Occipital headache upon awakening, shortness of breath, chest pain, visual changes

Symptoms are usually absent early; when present, they suggest end-organ damage or severe hypertension.

**Q:** What is the management of hypertension based on underlying disorder?

**A:** Treatment is individualized based on etiology, comorbidities, and severity

See updated guidelines at http://guidelines.hypertension.ca/ for current recommendations.

**Q:** What are the blood pressure thresholds for hypertension diagnosis?

**A:** Diabetic: office BP >130/80 mmHg; Non-diabetic (AOBP): >135/85 mmHg or OBPM ≥140/90 mmHg; ABPM daytime: >135/85 mmHg or 24hr mean >130/80 mmHg

Hypertension definitions vary by measurement method and diabetic status. White coat hypertension must be ruled out.

**Q:** Why are symptoms usually absent in hypertension?

**A:** Hypertension is typically asymptomatic because there are no specific symptoms; patients may have an occipital headache upon awakening or no symptoms at all until organ damage occurs

This is why hypertension is called the 'silent killer' and regular screening is essential.

**Q:** What is the target blood pressure for diabetics?

**A:** Less than 130/80 mmHg

Optimal blood pressure control for diabetics is <130/80 to reduce cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What medications are considered for cardiovascular protection in diabetics?

**A:** ACE-I/ARB, Statin, ASA

Diabetics with cardiovascular risk should consider ACE inhibitors/ARBs, statins, and aspirin for cardioprotection.

**Q:** What is the definition of hypertension in diabetic patients?

**A:** Office BP >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days

Diabetic patients have lower threshold - target is tighter for cardiovascular protection.

**Q:** What is the definition of hypertension in non-diabetic patients?

**A:** AOBP >135/85 mmHg OR OBPM ≥140/90 mmHg, confirmed on different days

Confirmation on multiple visits rules out white coat hypertension before treatment.

**Q:** What defines hypertension on ambulatory BP monitoring?

**A:** ABPM daytime mean >135/85 mmHg OR 24hr mean >130/80 mmHg

ABPM is gold standard for confirming true hypertension vs white coat effect.

**A:** Usually asymptomatic; may have occipital headache on awakening or organ-specific symptoms

Hypertension is often called 'silent killer' - screening essential as most patients have no symptoms.

**A:** Office BP measurement >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days

Diabetic patients have a lower threshold for hypertension diagnosis and treatment due to increased cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What is the blood pressure threshold for hypertension diagnosis in non-diabetic patients?

**A:** Automated office BP >135/85 mmHg or office BP ≥140/90 mmHg

Non-diabetic patients are diagnosed with hypertension at higher thresholds than diabetics.

**Q:** What are the ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) criteria for hypertension?

**A:** Daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg

ABPM provides a more accurate assessment by eliminating white coat effect and measuring true ambulatory blood pressure.

**Q:** What is white coat hypertension?

**A:** Elevated office BP measurements in patients with normal BP outside the clinical setting

White coat hypertension should be ruled out by confirming with ABPM or home BP monitoring before diagnosing true hypertension.

**A:** Usually asymptomatic; may have occipital headache upon awakening or organ-specific symptoms

Most patients are asymptomatic, which is why hypertension is often called the 'silent killer'; symptoms typically only appear with severe elevation or end-organ damage.

**A:** ABPM daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or ABPM 24 hr mean >130/80 mmHg

This is why hypertension is called the 'silent killer.' Symptoms only appear with severe elevation or end-organ damage.

**A:** <130/80 mmHg

Blood pressure control is crucial for reducing cardiovascular complications in diabetic patients.

**A:** Office BP >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days

Diabetics have lower BP targets due to increased cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic thresholds for hypertension using different methods?

**A:** AOBP >135/85 mmHg or OBPM ≥140/90 mmHg; ABPM daytime >135/85 mmHg or 24hr >130/80 mmHg

Multiple measurement methods exist; ABPM is gold standard for confirming diagnosis.

**Q:** What is the blood pressure threshold for hypertension in diabetic patients?

**A:** Office BP >130/80 mmHg on ≥3 different days

In diabetic patients, office BP >130/80 mmHg on at least 3 different days suggests probable hypertension.

**Q:** What is the blood pressure threshold for hypertension in non-diabetic patients using automated office BP?

**A:** AOBP >135/85 mmHg or OBPM ≥140/90 mmHg

For non-diabetic patients, hypertension is defined as AOBP >135/85 mmHg or office BP ≥140/90 mmHg.

**Q:** What is the ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) threshold for hypertension?

**A:** Daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg

ABPM defines hypertension as daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg.

**A:** Usually no symptoms; may have occipital headache upon awakening or organ-specific symptoms

HTN is usually asymptomatic; patients may present with occipital headache on awakening or symptoms of end-organ damage.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension in patients with diabetes?

**A:** Office BP measurement >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days, after ruling out white coat hypertension

Lower thresholds are used for diabetic patients due to increased cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension in non-diabetic patients?

**A:** Automated office BP (AOBP) >135/85 mmHg or office BP measurement (OBPM) >140/90 mmHg, after ruling out white coat hypertension

These thresholds apply to non-diabetic adults for hypertension diagnosis.

**Q:** What is the optimal blood pressure control target in diabetes?

**A:** <130/80 mmHg

Blood pressure should be controlled to below 130/80 mmHg in patients with diabetes to reduce cardiovascular risk.

**Q:** What is the target blood pressure for diabetes patients?

**A:** Less than 130/80 mmHg

BP target <130/80 reduces cardiovascular and renal complications in diabetic patients.

**Q:** What are the SMART goals for diabetes management?

**A:** A1C: Optimal <7%, BP: Optimal <130/80, Cholesterol: LDL-C <2 mmol/L if treating, consider ACEI/ARB, Statin, ASA, Exercise/Eating, Smoking Cessation

SMART goals provide targets for comprehensive diabetes management to reduce complications.

**Q:** What medications are recommended for diabetes patients with cardiovascular risk?

**A:** Consider ACEI/ARB (for blood pressure), Statin (for cholesterol), ASA (for antiplatelet effect)

Cardiovascular protection is a key component of diabetes management with these medication classes.

**Q:** What is the diagnostic threshold for hypertension in diabetic patients?

**A:** Office BP measurement >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days = probable hypertension (rule out white coat)

Diabetic patients have lower BP targets due to increased cardiovascular risk

**Q:** What is the diagnostic threshold for hypertension in non-diabetic patients?

**A:** Automated office BP >135/85 mmHg OR office BP ≥140/90 mmHg = probable hypertension (rule out white coat)

Confirmation requires excluding white coat hypertension

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension using ABPM and home BP?

**A:** ABPM daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24hr mean >130/80 mmHg = hypertension. Home BP monitoring criteria also available

Ambulatory and home monitoring help confirm true hypertension and rule out white coat

**Q:** What was the DASH trial studying and what was its conclusion?

**A:** The DASH trial showed that a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products significantly reduces blood pressure - by 11.4/5.5 mmHg in hypertensive patients and 5.5/3.0 mmHg in normotensive patients

The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet is now a cornerstone recommendation for blood pressure management.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension (HTN) in non-diabetic patients?

**A:** Automated office BP >135/85 mmHg OR office BP >140/90 mmHg on 3 separate days, confirmed by home BP or ABPM

Multiple measurements on different days confirm diagnosis; white coat hypertension must be ruled out before treatment.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension in diabetic patients?

**A:** Office BP >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days

Diabetic patients have lower BP targets due to increased cardiovascular risk; white coat HTN should still be ruled out.

**Q:** What are the ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) criteria for diagnosing hypertension?

**A:** Daytime mean >135/85 mmHg OR 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg

ABPM provides more accurate diagnosis by eliminating white coat effect and assessing diurnal patterns; correlates better with outcomes.

**Q:** What are the symptoms of hypertension?

**A:** Usually no symptoms; patients may have occipital headache upon awakening or organ-specific symptoms

Hypertension is often asymptomatic, which is why it is called the 'silent killer'.

**Q:** What are the diagnostic criteria for hypertension in diabetic vs. non-diabetic patients?

**A:** Diabetic: office BP >130/80 mmHg for ≥3 measurements on different days. Non-diabetic: automated office BP >135/85 mmHg or office BP ≥140/90 mmHg. Confirm with ABPM: daytime mean >135/85 mmHg or 24-hour mean >130/80 mmHg

Lower thresholds apply to diabetic patients due to increased cardiovascular risk. Home BP monitoring and ABPM help rule out white coat hypertension.

**Q:** What was the DASH trial and what diet showed the best blood pressure reduction?

**A:** DASH trial (NEJM 1997): A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products (combination diet) reduced BP more than control or fruits/vegetables alone - 5.5/3.0 mmHg in normotensive and 11.4/5.5 mmHg in hypertensive patients

The DASH diet is now recommended as first-line lifestyle intervention for hypertension and prehypertension.

**Q:** What did the SPRINT trial demonstrate about intensive blood pressure control?

**A:** Intensive treatment (target SBP <120 mmHg) vs. standard (<140 mmHg) significantly reduced cardiovascular events (1.65%/year vs 2.19%/year) in high-risk patients over 3 years

SPRINT showed that more intensive BP control in high-risk patients reduces major cardiovascular complications and mortality.

**Q:** What antibiotics cover ascending cholangitis?

**A:** Broad spectrum covering Gram-negatives, Enterococcus, and anaerobes: ampicillin+sulbactam, piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole+3rd gen cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone, or carbapenem monotherapy

Antibiotic choice should cover the typical organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Enterococcus) and anaerobes, especially during CBD manipulation.

**Q:** What are the late-stage signs of Primary Biliary Cholangitis?

**A:** Jaundice, melanosis (darkening skin), xanthelasma, hepatocellular failure, portal hypertension, ascites

Chronic cholestasis leads to skin changes, xanthelasma (yellow bumps around eyes), and eventually end-stage liver disease with failure and portal hypertension.

**Q:** What antibiotics should be considered for Ascending Cholangitis?

**A:** Broad spectrum covering Gram-negatives, Enterococcus, and anaerobes: ampicillin+sulbactam, piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole+3rd gen cephalosporin/fluoroquinolone, or carbapenem monotherapy

Coverage must include E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Enterococcus, and anaerobes (especially after CBD manipulation).

**Q:** What complications are associated with PBC?

**A:** High incidence of osteoporosis, hepatocellular failure, portal hypertension, ascites

Chronic cholestasis leads to malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins and bone loss. End-stage disease results in liver failure and portal hypertension.

**Q:** What antibiotics are used for ascending cholangitis?

**A:** Ampicillin + sulbactam OR piperacillin/tazobactam; OR metronidazole + 3rd generation cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone; OR carbapenem monotherapy

Coverage must include Gram-negatives, Enterococcus, and anaerobes, especially during CBD manipulation

**Q:** What is clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in cirrhosis?

**A:** Portal hypertension sufficient to increase risk of decompensation, typically defined by hepatic venous pressure gradient ≥10 mmHg

CSPH represents the threshold at which patients with compensated cirrhosis become at risk for decompensation events like ascites, varices, or hepatic encephalopathy.

**Q:** What is the definition of clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH)?

**A:** Hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) ≥10 mmHg, associated with increased risk of decompensation.

CSPH (HVPG ≥10 mmHg) marks the threshold at which patients with cirrhosis develop varices and are at risk for decompensation events like ascites and variceal bleeding.

**Q:** What are the late-stage complications of Primary Biliary Cholangitis?

**A:** Hepatocellular failure, portal hypertension, and ascites

End-stage PBC leads to liver failure and complications of portal hypertension due to chronic cholestasis and fibrosis.

**Q:** What is clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) defined as in the PREDESCI trial?

**A:** Hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) ≥10 mmHg

CSPH is a key predictor of cirrhosis decompensation and is defined hemodynamically by an HVPG of 10 mmHg or greater.

**Q:** What is clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in the context of cirrhosis?

**A:** Portal hypertension with hepatic venous pressure gradient ≥10 mmHg, associated with increased risk of cirrhosis decompensation

CSPH is defined by a hepatic venous pressure gradient of 10 mmHg or higher and marks the transition from compensated to decompensated cirrhosis risk.

**Q:** What are the risk factors for wound hemorrhage and hematoma?

**A:** Anticoagulant therapy, coagulopathies, thrombocytopenia, DIC, severe liver disease, myeloproliferative disorders, severe arterial hypertension, and severe cough; more common with transverse muscle incisions.

These conditions impair hemostasis or increase pressure on the wound, leading to bleeding into the surgical site.

**Q:** What foods should be avoided in gout (mnemonic)?

**A:** FACT - Feverfew, Alcohol, Cyclosporine, Thiazide diuretics; and SALT - Seafood, Alcohol, Liver, Turkey

These foods and drugs can precipitate gout attacks by increasing uric acid levels or reducing excretion.

**Q:** What is the mnemonic for gout precipitants?

**A:** FACT (Feverfew, Alcohol, Cyclosporine, Thiazide) and SALT (Seafood, Alcohol, Liver, Turkey)

These help remember common triggers that can precipitate acute gout attacks.

**Q:** What are the indications for surgical treatment of vesicoureteral reflux?

**A:** Failure of medical management, renal scarring (renal insufficiency, hypertension), breakthrough UTIs, or persistent high-grade (IV or V) reflux

Surgical options include ureteral reimplantation or subureteric injection with bulking agents (Deflux or Macroplastique).

**Q:** What receptor does clonidine act on, and what is its primary clinical use?

**A:** Alpha-2 (a2) agonist; primary use is hypertension (also used for opioid/alcohol withdrawal and ADHD)

Clonidine stimulates central a2 receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow and lowering blood pressure. It can cause rebound hypertension upon abrupt discontinuation. Methyldopa, another a2 agonist, is safe in pregnancy for hypertension management.

**Q:** Beta-1 selective adrenergic blockers (e.g., metoprolol, atenolol) are preferred over non-selective beta-blockers in patients with which comorbidity?

**A:** Reactive airway disease (asthma/COPD) — beta-1 selective agents have less bronchospasm risk than non-selective agents like propranolol

Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, timolol) block both B1 and B2 receptors; B2 blockade causes bronchoconstriction. Cardioselective (B1-selective) agents like metoprolol and atenolol are relatively safer in obstructive airway disease but should still be used cautiously.

**Q:** SPRINT trial compared intensive SBP control (<120 mmHg) to standard control (<140 mmHg) in high-CV-risk patients without diabetes. What was found?

**A:** Intensive BP control (<120 mmHg) significantly reduced major CV events and all-cause mortality compared to standard control (<140 mmHg)

SPRINT (NEJM 2015) showed intensive SBP control reduced the primary composite by 25% (HR 0.75) and all-cause mortality by 27% (HR 0.73) in non-diabetic high-CV-risk patients. This influenced Canadian Hypertension guidelines toward lower BP targets.

**Q:** HYVET trial studied antihypertensive treatment in patients aged >80 with SBP >160. What was the key finding?

**A:** Indapamide (with or without perindopril) reduced stroke risk, stroke death, and all-cause mortality in patients over 80 with hypertension

HYVET (NEJM 2008) demonstrated that treating hypertension in octogenarians with indapamide SR 2.5 mg (±perindopril) resulted in a 30% reduction in stroke and 21% reduction in all-cause mortality. This challenged the previous concern that aggressive BP treatment in the elderly was harmful.

**Q:** What is the key difference between alpha-1 (a1) and alpha-2 (a2) receptor effects on cardiovascular physiology?

**A:** a1 receptors cause vasoconstriction of skin, skeletal muscle, and splanchnic vessels with increased myocardial contractility; a2 receptors peripherally modulate vessel tone (both vasoconstrict and dilate) and decrease HR

a1 blockade (e.g., prazosin) reduces peripheral vascular resistance and is used in hypertension. a2 agonism (e.g., clonidine) reduces central sympathetic outflow. Understanding receptor subtypes guides selection of adrenergic drugs in clinical practice.

**Q:** Define hypertensive emergency and name the end organs that can be damaged.

**A:** Severe BP elevation with evidence of end-organ damage. Affected organs: CNS (stroke, encephalopathy, seizures), retinal (hemorrhage, papilledema), cardiovascular (dissection, ACS, CHF), renal (elevated creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria), GI (N/V, elevated liver enzymes). In pregnancy: HELLP syndrome.

The key distinction from hypertensive urgency (asymptomatic severe HTN) is end-organ damage. The degree of BP elevation alone does not define an emergency—it is the presence of target organ injury that mandates urgent treatment.

**Q:** What is the BP reduction strategy for hypertensive emergency?

**A:** Lower BP by 25% over the initial 60 minutes, then gradually over 24-48 hours. Do NOT rapidly normalize BP (risk of ischemia to adapted organs).

Chronically hypertensive patients have autoregulatory curves shifted to tolerate higher BP. Rapid normalization removes perfusion pressure from vital organs, causing ischemic stroke, AKI, or coronary ischemia. Exception: aortic dissection requires rapid reduction of sBP to 110-120 mmHg STAT.

**Q:** Why are non-selective beta-blockers avoided in hypertensive emergencies caused by cocaine/pheochromocytoma?

**A:** They block β-mediated vasodilation while leaving α-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening hypertension. Use phentolamine (α-blocker) instead.

In states of catecholamine excess (cocaine, pheochromocytoma), both α- and β-receptors are stimulated. β-blockers only block vasodilation (β2), allowing the pressor α1 effect to dominate, causing a paradoxical BP rise. Labetalol (combined α+β blocker) is acceptable, or use phentolamine for pure α-blockade.

**Q:** What is the management of hypertensive emergency in aortic dissection?

**A:** Rapid reduction of sBP to 110-120 mmHg STAT. Use esmolol + sodium nitroprusside. Do NOT resuscitate with IV fluids.

Aortic dissection is propagated by high BP and aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt). Unlike other hypertensive emergencies, the goal is rapid—not gradual—BP reduction. Esmolol controls heart rate and reduces dP/dt; nitroprusside (or nicardipine) reduces afterload. IV fluids increase cardiac output and worsen dissection.

**Q:** What is the initial drug of choice for most hypertensive emergencies and what are its contraindications?

**A:** Labetalol (IV). Contraindications: acute CHF, heart block >1st degree, severe asthma (relative).

Labetalol is a combined α1 + β (nonselective) blocker that reduces BP without causing reflex tachycardia. It is preferred in most hypertensive emergencies including eclampsia. Its onset is 5-10 minutes and duration is 3-6 hours. It should be avoided in acute decompensated CHF (β-blockade worsens cardiac output).

**Q:** According to CTFPHC guidelines, what is the recommended blood pressure measurement standard for the periodic health examination?

**A:** BP measurement should be performed using techniques described in CHEP (Canadian Hypertension Education Program) guidelines (Grade A recommendation in PHE table).

The CHEP guidelines specify proper BP measurement technique: patient seated quietly for 5 minutes, two measurements taken at least 1 minute apart, automated oscillometric devices preferred for office measurement, and out-of-office (home or ambulatory) BP measurement to confirm hypertension diagnosis. This is a Grade A recommendation in the Canadian PHE.

**Q:** What are the key results and conclusion of the DASH trial?

**A:** The DASH diet (combination diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy) reduced systolic/diastolic BP by 5.5/3.0 mmHg in normotensive patients and by 11.4/5.5 mmHg in hypertensive patients compared to a control diet. Conclusion: Dietary modification can significantly reduce blood pressure.

The DASH trial demonstrated that dietary patterns have a clinically meaningful effect on blood pressure. This supports lifestyle modification as first-line management for hypertension, consistent with Canadian Hypertension guidelines (Hypertension Canada).

**Q:** What was the SPRINT trial and what were its key findings?

**A:** SPRINT (2015) compared intensive BP target (systolic <120 mmHg) vs. standard target (<140 mmHg) in 9,361 high-CV-risk patients. Results: intensive treatment reduced CV complications (1.65%/yr vs. 2.19%/yr). Conclusion: Intensive BP control in high-risk patients reduces major CV events.

SPRINT influenced guidelines supporting lower BP targets (systolic <120 mmHg) in high-CV-risk patients. However, the method of BP measurement (unattended automated) differs from typical office measurement, a key contextual point for the MCCQE1.

## Valvular Heart Disease

**Q:** A 75-year-old has exertional syncope, angina, and dyspnea. Harsh systolic murmur at right upper sternal border radiating to neck. Echo: AVA 0.8 cm2, mean gradient 45 mmHg. Diagnosis and management?

**A:** Severe aortic stenosis; SAVR or TAVR depending on surgical risk — symptomatic severe AS has 2-year mortality ~50% without intervention

CCS guidelines recommend intervention for symptomatic severe AS (AVA <1.0 cm2, mean gradient >40 mmHg). TAVR for high-risk/inoperable; SAVR preferred for low-risk patients <65.

**Q:** What physical exam findings characterize mitral stenosis?

**A:** Opening snap after S2, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at apex, loud S1, signs of pulmonary hypertension

Mitral stenosis is most commonly rheumatic. Severity: MVA <1.0 cm2 = severe. AF common due to LA enlargement. Treatment: diuretics, anticoagulation if AF, balloon mitral valvuloplasty, or MVR.

**Q:** A 40-year-old with bicuspid aortic valve has severe AR. Echo shows LVEDD 65mm, LVESD 45mm, EF 55%. When to recommend surgery?

**A:** Surgery for severe AR with: EF <50%, LVEDD >70mm, LVESD >50mm, or symptoms

CCS guidelines recommend AVR for symptomatic severe AR or asymptomatic meeting echocardiographic thresholds. Vasodilators temporize but do not replace surgery. Surveillance echo every 6-12 months.

**Q:** What is the Carpentier classification of mitral regurgitation?

**A:** Type I: normal leaflet motion (annular dilation, perforation); Type II: excessive motion (prolapse, chordal rupture); Type III: restricted motion (rheumatic IIIa, ischemic IIIb)

Understanding MR mechanism guides surgical approach. Type II MR is most amenable to repair. CCS prefers mitral valve repair over replacement. Surgery for severe MR with symptoms or EF <60% or LVESD >40mm.

**Q:** What antibiotic is used for IE prophylaxis before dental procedures in high-risk patients?

**A:** Amoxicillin 2g PO 30-60 min before procedure (clindamycin 600mg if penicillin allergic)

Prophylaxis only for high-risk conditions: prosthetic valve, prior IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD. NOT recommended for MVP alone or most native valve disease — significant narrowing of indications from prior guidelines.

**Q:** A 65-year-old with MVP has sudden severe MR and flail posterior leaflet on echo after minor chest trauma. Management?

**A:** Urgent mitral valve surgery (repair if feasible); stabilize with IV nitroprusside and diuretics as bridge

Acute severe MR causes volume overload of non-dilated LV, rapid hemodynamic deterioration. Nitroprusside reduces afterload and improves forward flow. IABP can bridge to OR.

**Q:** What are the major Duke criteria for infective endocarditis?

**A:** Positive blood cultures (typical organisms x2 or persistent bacteremia) AND evidence of endocardial involvement (echo vegetation, new regurgitation, positive Q-gate CT)

Definite IE: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. TOE preferred for sensitivity. Blood cultures (3 sets before antibiotics) are critical.

**Q:** Common organisms in native valve vs. prosthetic valve endocarditis?

**A:** Native valve: Strep viridans (subacute), Staph aureus (acute), Enterococcus; Early prosthetic (<60d): CoNS, Staph aureus; Late prosthetic (>60d): similar to native

Strep viridans causes subacute IE via dental portals. Staph aureus causes acute IE with rapid valve destruction. IV drug use: Staph aureus, right-sided (tricuspid). Duration: 4-6 weeks IV antibiotics.

**Q:** A patient with mechanical mitral valve has INR 6.5 and minor bleeding. Management?

**A:** Hold warfarin, give vitamin K 1-2.5 mg PO; if major bleeding: 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K — DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves

Mechanical valves require lifelong anticoagulation (INR 2.5-3.5 for mitral). DOACs contraindicated with mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN trial showed increased thromboembolism).

**Q:** What cardiac manifestations are associated with Marfan syndrome?

**A:** Aortic root dilation/dissection (major cause of death) and mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation

Prophylactic aortic root repair when diameter ≥5.0 cm. Beta-blockers and losartan slow aortic expansion. Annual surveillance MRI/CT of aorta.

**Q:** A 72-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of exertional syncope, dyspnea, and angina. Auscultation reveals a harsh systolic murmur that peaks late and a single S2. Carotid upstroke is slow and delayed. Echo shows a peak gradient of 90 mmHg, mean gradient 62 mmHg, AVA 0.6 cm², and EF 62%. What is the immediate management?

A) Aortic valvuloplasty as a bridge to definitive therapy
B) Urgent surgical aortic valve replacement
C) TAVR based on age and hemodynamics
D) Intensive medical therapy with diuretics and beta-blockade

**A:** B) Urgent surgical aortic valve replacement

This patient has severe symptomatic AS with classic triad (syncope, angina, dyspnea). Mean gradient ≥40 mmHg + AVA ≤0.6 cm² = very severe AS. The symptom triad carries a prognosis of death within 2–5 years without AVR. In a 72-year-old with no stated surgical contraindications, SAVR is the gold standard (durability, leaflet anatomy). TAVR is preferred for high surgical risk (STS ≥ 8%) or intermediate risk if anatomy favors TAVR (PARTNER 2, SURTAVI). Age 72 with no comorbidities listed = likely low-intermediate risk — SAVR is the standard. Guidelines do not recommend medical therapy to delay AVR in symptomatic severe AS.

**Q:** A 65-year-old woman has asymptomatic severe AS (peak velocity 5.2 m/s, mean gradient 68 mmHg, AVA 0.65 cm², EF 55%). She is being managed conservatively. Which finding would prompt intervention BEFORE symptom development?

A) Peak velocity of 5.2 m/s alone — very severe AS warrants prophylactic intervention
B) Progressive decline in EF from 55% to 52% over 12 months
C) LVEF falling below 50%
D) Rate of Vmax increase > 0.3 m/s/year on serial echo

**A:** C) LVEF falling below 50%

Per 2021 ESC and 2020 ACC/AHA guidelines, AVR in ASYMPTOMATIC severe AS is recommended when: (1) LVEF < 50% (Class I) — systolic dysfunction is occurring; (2) very severe AS (Vmax ≥ 5.0 m/s) with low surgical risk (Class IIa, ESC). Recent AVATAR and RECOVERY trials support early AVR in very severe asymptomatic AS. A Vmax of 5.2 m/s + any LVEF drop below 50% is a Class I indication. EF dropping from 55% to 52% is concerning but not yet the 50% threshold. LVEF < 50% is the clearest non-symptom surgical trigger.

**Q:** A 48-year-old man has severe aortic regurgitation. Echo shows: EF 52%, LVESD 51mm, LVEDD 72mm. He is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?

A) Medical therapy with vasodilators — surgery not yet required
B) Aortic valve replacement — LVESD ≥ 50mm is a surgical indication
C) Annual surveillance echo — below all surgical thresholds
D) Aortic valve repair — preferred over replacement in regurgitation

**A:** B) Aortic valve replacement — LVESD ≥ 50mm is a surgical indication

Per 2020 ACC/AHA guidelines for severe aortic regurgitation, AVR is recommended (Class I) for: (1) symptomatic patients; (2) LVEF < 55%; (3) LVESD ≥ 50mm (Class IIa) — per 2014 guidelines. The 2020 ACC/AHA guideline updates: AVR is Class IIa when LVESD > 50mm OR LVESD index > 25mm/m² in asymptomatic patients. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend surgery when LVESD > 50mm. This patient has LVESD 51mm — a Class IIa/Class I threshold depending on the guideline used. Given borderline EF 52% approaching the <55% threshold and LVESD ≥ 50mm, surgical referral is appropriate.

**Q:** A 35-year-old woman, para 2, develops severe dyspnea in the third trimester. Echo shows mitral stenosis with MVA 0.9 cm², mean gradient 18 mmHg, Wilkins score 6. She has mild mitral regurgitation (1+) and no LAA thrombus. What is the most appropriate intervention?

A) Urgent caesarean section and simultaneous mitral valve replacement under cardiopulmonary bypass
B) Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty (PMBV) — safe in pregnancy with favorable anatomy
C) Medical management with diuretics and beta-blockers until delivery
D) Heart rate control with bisoprolol; delay all procedural intervention until postpartum

**A:** B) Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty (PMBV) — safe in pregnancy with favorable anatomy

Severe MS (MVA <1.0 cm²) with NYHA III/IV in pregnancy is a high-risk situation. PMBV is the treatment of choice for severe symptomatic MS in pregnancy when: (1) anatomy is favorable (Wilkins score ≤8), (2) no significant MR, (3) no LAA thrombus. Wilkins score 6 + mild MR + no thrombus = ideal for PMBV. MVR under CPB carries 15–30% fetal mortality and significant maternal risk. Surgical intervention is a last resort. PMBV can be safely performed with lead shielding to minimize fetal radiation exposure (ideally after week 12). Beta-blockers and diuretics help but are insufficient for severe hemodynamic compromise.

**Q:** A 68-year-old man with a history of rheumatic fever has mixed mitral valve disease. Echo shows mean MV gradient 12 mmHg, MVA 1.3 cm² (moderate MS), and grade 3/4 MR. EF is 50%. He is NYHA class III. What is the most appropriate surgical intervention?

A) Mitral valve repair targeting the MR component only
B) Mitral valve replacement — combined MS/MR with rheumatic etiology is not repairable
C) Mitral balloon valvuloplasty — the MS component is dominant
D) Transcatheter MV replacement (TMVR) via TENDYNE or Intrepid system

**A:** B) Mitral valve replacement — combined MS/MR with rheumatic etiology is not repairable

In rheumatic mixed mitral valve disease (moderate MS + significant MR), the valve leaflets and subvalvular apparatus are typically heavily fibrosed and calcified — making repair technically unfeasible with high recurrence rates. MVR (mitral valve replacement) is the definitive surgical treatment. Unlike degenerative MR (where repair rates > 95% in expert centres), rheumatic MV disease has much lower repair rates. The combination of MS + MR with rheumatic pathology, NYHA III, and declining EF (approaching 50%) is a clear MVR indication. TMVR is an emerging option for high-risk surgical patients.

**Q:** A 74-year-old woman has severe aortic stenosis (AVA 0.7 cm²) and is being evaluated for TAVR. Her CT aortogram shows a bicuspid aortic valve (type 1 fusion, no raphe), aortic annulus diameter 26mm, and LVOT calcification (calcium volume 1200 mm³). What is the major risk associated with TAVR in this patient?

A) Higher risk of vascular access complications due to large annulus
B) Increased risk of paravalvular regurgitation and annular rupture
C) No increased risk — bicuspid AS is no longer a contraindication to TAVR
D) Bicuspid valve is more prone to TAVR device embolization into the aorta

**A:** B) Increased risk of paravalvular regurgitation and annular rupture

Bicuspid AS presents specific TAVR challenges: (1) Elliptical/asymmetric annular anatomy makes sizing difficult — increased risk of paravalvular regurgitation (PVL); (2) Heavy asymmetric calcium (especially LVOT calcium, calcium volume > 800mm³) → risk of annular rupture during balloon post-dilation; (3) Coronary height and commissure alignment issues; (4) Supra-annular calcium may prevent full expansion. LVOT calcium > 800mm³ is a predictor of device success and annular rupture. Large bicuspid annuli (>26mm) may exceed TAVR prosthesis sizing limits. Surgical AVR remains preferred in low-risk bicuspid patients at experienced centres.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man has recently recovered from S. aureus bacteremia. He was treated with IV nafcillin for 6 weeks for aortic valve endocarditis. Echo shows a mobile vegetation on the aortic valve but no hemodynamic compromise. He remains afebrile and blood cultures have been negative for 2 weeks. When is it safe to consider valve surgery (AVR) in this patient?

A) Immediate surgery — S. aureus endocarditis always requires surgical debridement
B) Wait 4–6 weeks post-bacteremia clearance before proceeding with AVR
C) Surgery is not indicated — he has been treated; surveillance echo every 3 months
D) Proceed with surgery now to eradicate residual vegetation and prevent embolism

**A:** D) Proceed with surgery now to eradicate residual vegetation and prevent embolism

In NVE (native valve endocarditis), the principal indications for surgery during active infection include: (1) Heart failure (HF from severe valve regurgitation); (2) Uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteremia, abscess, fistula); (3) Prevention of embolism (large vegetation > 10mm + prior embolic event, or > 15mm with mobile vegetation especially on anterior MV leaflet). S. aureus NVE with a persistent mobile vegetation carries high embolic risk (CVA, visceral infarction). Despite clinical improvement, the presence of a mobile vegetation in S. aureus endocarditis supports EARLY surgical intervention to prevent catastrophic embolization.

**Q:** A 63-year-old man had mechanical aortic valve replacement 5 years ago. He takes warfarin with a target INR of 2.5–3.5. He requires urgent abdominal surgery. His last INR was 3.2 yesterday. How should anticoagulation be managed?

A) Hold warfarin and bridge with LMWH (therapeutic dose) until surgery
B) Give IV vitamin K 10mg to rapidly reverse INR, then bridge with UFH
C) Proceed with surgery with INR 3.2 — mechanical valves are a relative contraindication to reversal
D) Give 4-factor PCC to fully reverse, proceed with urgent surgery, restart warfarin 24h post-op

**A:** D) Give 4-factor PCC to fully reverse, proceed with urgent surgery, restart warfarin 24h post-op

For urgent/emergent surgery with a mechanical heart valve on warfarin, the decision depends on urgency. For URGENT (same-day/emergency) surgery with INR 3.2: 4-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg) rapidly reverses INR within minutes (1–2 hours) — superior to FFP for urgent reversal. Adding low-dose IV vitamin K (1–2mg) helps maintain reversal. Post-operatively, restart warfarin and bridge with UFH until therapeutic. LMWH bridging for mechanical valves is inferior to UFH (evidence from BRIDGE trial supports no bridging in bioprosthetic/low-risk AF, but mechanical valves always require bridging). 4-PCC is the fastest reversal agent for urgent scenarios.

**Q:** A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus has a murmur. Echo shows: Mitral valve with nodular thickening on both surfaces of the leaflets (Libman-Sacks), mild mitral regurgitation, small pericardial effusion. She is asymptomatic. Blood cultures are negative. Which statement is MOST accurate?

A) Libman-Sacks endocarditis is an indication for immediate surgical valve replacement
B) The vegetations are sterile fibrin thrombi; antibiotic prophylaxis is required pre-procedure
C) The main risk of Libman-Sacks endocarditis is peripheral embolism; anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated
D) This is always associated with antiphospholipid syndrome; DOAC is preferred for anticoagulation

**A:** C) The main risk of Libman-Sacks endocarditis is peripheral embolism; anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) in SLE consists of sterile, fibrinous (non-infectious) vegetations occurring on both leaflet surfaces — characteristically on the ventricular surface of the mitral valve (differentiating from infectious endocarditis on atrial surface). The main complications are embolic (CVA, TIA, peripheral). Anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated in SLE patients with LSE + antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) — DOACs are NOT recommended in antiphospholipid syndrome (TRAPS trial showed worse outcomes with rivaroxaban vs. warfarin in triple-positive APS). Surgery is reserved for significant hemodynamic compromise.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man presents with acute severe MR following rupture of a chordae tendineae. Echo shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet P2 scallop, severe MR (jet eccentric, hugging the left atrial wall), LVEF 65%, and LVEDV mildly dilated. BP is 95/60, HR 120. What is the most appropriate hemodynamic optimization BEFORE surgery?

A) Phenylephrine to increase BP and afterload
B) IV nitroprusside or nitroglycerin ± IABP to reduce afterload and forward flow
C) IV metoprolol to control heart rate
D) IV fluid challenge to increase preload and stroke volume

**A:** B) IV nitroprusside or nitroglycerin ± IABP to reduce afterload and forward flow

In acute severe MR, the dilated, thin-walled left atrium cannot accommodate the acute volume overload — pulmonary edema ensues. The regurgitant fraction depends heavily on the pressure gradient between LV and LA, and LV outflow resistance (afterload). Reducing afterload (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin) decreases the regurgitant fraction and increases forward cardiac output. IABP can augment forward flow and reduce afterload in cardiogenic shock. Phenylephrine increases SVR → more blood regurgitates back into LA (contraindicated). Fluid challenge worsens pulmonary edema. The definitive treatment is urgent surgical MV repair.

**Q:** A 70-year-old man undergoes TAVR for severe AS. On post-procedure echo, Doppler shows a peak gradient of 28 mmHg across the TAVR prosthesis (expected < 20 mmHg for valve size), moderate prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM) by effective orifice area index (0.63 cm²/m²). He is dyspneic on exertion post-procedure. What does PPM represent?

A) The transcatheter valve leaflets are malfunctioning — requires redo TAVR
B) The prosthetic valve is functioning normally but is too small for the patient's hemodynamic demands
C) Pannus ingrowth has already occurred, causing valve obstruction
D) Subclinical leaflet thrombosis — anticoagulation is required

**A:** B) The prosthetic valve is functioning normally but is too small for the patient's hemodynamic demands

Prosthesis-Patient Mismatch (PPM) occurs when a normally functioning prosthetic valve is hemodynamically too small for the patient's body surface area/cardiac output requirements — the effective orifice area (EOA) indexed to BSA is less than what the native heart requires. Moderate PPM: EOAI 0.65–0.85 cm²/m²; severe PPM < 0.65 cm²/m². This is distinct from structural valve dysfunction. PPM contributes to residual gradients and reduced functional improvement post-AVR/TAVR. It is associated with worse outcomes. Prevention: using the largest possible prosthesis (annular enlargement in surgery, largest TAVR for annulus). No further intervention needed — consider exercise tolerance management.

**Q:** A 78-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic mitral valve (implanted 9 years ago) presents with worsening exertional dyspnea. Echo shows: mean mitral gradient 18 mmHg (previously 6 mmHg two years ago), valve area by PHT 0.9 cm², normal EF. She is high risk for redo surgery (STS 9%). What is the most appropriate intervention?

A) Conservative management — bioprosthetic valve stenosis is expected at 9 years
B) Redo MVR via sternotomy — transcatheter options not applicable to mitral bioprostheses
C) Valve-in-valve TMVR (transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve) using TAVR technology
D) Balloon valvuloplasty of the bioprosthetic valve

**A:** C) Valve-in-valve TMVR (transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve) using TAVR technology

Transcatheter valve-in-valve (ViV) TMVR is an established procedure for failing bioprosthetic mitral valves in patients who are high surgical risk for redo operation. The technique deploys a TAVR prosthesis (typically a balloon-expandable valve like the SAPIEN 3) within the failed bioprosthesis, using the old valve's ring as the landing zone. Success rates are high with acceptable gradients. The MITRAL trial established feasibility. At STS 9%, redo conventional surgery carries prohibitive risk — ViV-TMVR is the guideline-supported alternative. Balloon valvuloplasty of a degenerated bioprosthesis causes leaflet destruction, not correction.

**Q:** A 30-year-old man has a bicuspid aortic valve incidentally found. He is asymptomatic with EF 65%, AVA 1.8 cm², and aortic root diameter of 46mm. His mother had a Type A aortic dissection at 50. Which surveillance and management plan is most appropriate?

A) Surveillance echo every 5 years — no action needed until AVA < 1.0 cm²
B) Annual echo and CT aorta — consider prophylactic aortic root surgery if diameter reaches 50mm
C) Annual echo; prophylactic surgery NOW given family history of dissection at aortic root diameter 46mm
D) Refer for genetic testing; elective AVR to eliminate bicuspid valve stress on the aortic root

**A:** B) Annual echo and CT aorta — consider prophylactic aortic root surgery if diameter reaches 50mm

Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is associated with aortopathy — dilation of the ascending aorta/root. Prophylactic surgery thresholds per 2022 ACC/AHA guidelines: aortic diameter ≥55mm (general), or ≥50mm with risk factors (family history of dissection, rapid growth >3mm/year, Marfan/Turner syndrome). At 46mm with family history, prophylactic surgery is not yet indicated. Annual surveillance imaging (TTE + CT aorta at 5-year intervals or sooner if growing) is appropriate. The threshold drops to 50mm with a first-degree relative with Type A dissection. This patient needs close monitoring but surgery at 46mm is premature.

**Q:** A 35-year-old man presents with sharp chest pain worse with inspiration and lying flat, improved by leaning forward. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression in multiple leads. His CRP is 85 mg/L. Troponin is mildly elevated (0.5 ng/mL). Echo shows no effusion. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

A) Aspirin 650mg q6h + colchicine 0.5mg BID + restrict strenuous exercise for 3 months
B) NSAID + prednisone — dual therapy is standard for pericarditis
C) Immediate drainage — elevated troponin indicates pericardial effusion
D) Heparin + aspirin — troponin elevation indicates concurrent MI

**A:** A) Aspirin 650mg q6h + colchicine 0.5mg BID + restrict strenuous exercise for 3 months

Acute pericarditis treatment: (1) Aspirin 750–1000mg TID or ibuprofen 600mg TID for 1–2 weeks with gradual taper; (2) Colchicine 0.5mg BID for 3 months (COPE, ICAP trials) — halves recurrence rate; (3) Exercise restriction until asymptomatic + CRP normalized (typically 3 months for athletes). Mild troponin elevation indicates myopericarditis (pericarditis with myocardial involvement) — does NOT change the pericarditis management and does not indicate MI or drainage. Corticosteroids are reserved for cases refractory to NSAID + colchicine or specific etiologies (connective tissue disease, autoreactive) — first-line steroids increase recurrence.

**Q:** A 65-year-old woman with lung cancer is found to have a large pericardial effusion on routine staging CT. Echo shows: RV diastolic collapse, RA systolic collapse, dilated IVC without respiratory variation. Her BP is 88/58, HR 120. What is the pathophysiology of her clinical state?

A) Elevated pericardial pressure reduces transmural filling pressure, impairing cardiac filling
B) The effusion directly compresses the coronary arteries, causing ischemia
C) Neurogenic activation of the Bezold-Jarisch reflex causes bradycardia and hypotension
D) The pericardial fluid increases LV afterload through visceral pericardial constriction

**A:** A) Elevated pericardial pressure reduces transmural filling pressure, impairing cardiac filling

Cardiac tamponade physiology: rising pericardial fluid raises intrapericardial pressure (IPP). When IPP equals the LOWEST diastolic filling pressure (usually RA, then RV), cardiac chambers collapse. Elevated IPP equalizes with RA and RV diastolic pressures → impaired ventricular filling → reduced CO → obstructive shock. The transmural pressure (intracavitary pressure minus pericardial pressure) falls to near zero. Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP. Classic signs: pulsus paradoxus > 10mmHg, electrical alternans, sinus tachycardia. Immediate pericardiocentesis is life-saving.

**Q:** A 55-year-old man presents 6 months after coronary artery bypass surgery with progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and lower extremity edema. JVP is elevated and does not decrease with inspiration (positive Kussmaul's sign). Heart sounds are normal. There is a pericardial knock on auscultation. Echo shows thickened pericardium with septal bounce and respiratory variation. What is the characteristic hemodynamic finding on right heart catheterization?

A) Elevated and equal diastolic pressures in all four chambers (diastolic equalization)
B) High PCWP with low CO and high SVR
C) High pulmonary artery systolic pressure with normal wedge
D) Normal RA pressure with elevated PCWP

**A:** A) Elevated and equal diastolic pressures in all four chambers (diastolic equalization)
